title: Balanced Ruck Stance and Ready Position
primarySkill: Ruck starting stance
objective: Develop a balanced and repeatable starting stance that allows a ruck to move, jump or protect space safely in any direction.
groundSize: One 4 × 4-metre working square for each group of two to four players.
coachingDifficulty: 1 – Simple organisation with minimal observation or intervention
setup:
Mark a 4 × 4-metre square for each group.
Place one coloured marker on each side of the square.
One player works in the middle while a partner or coach stands three metres away holding a football.
The working player begins in a neutral ruck stance facing the ball.
Allow at least two metres between neighbouring groups.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working player establishes a balanced stance with feet approximately shoulder-width apart, knees flexed and weight through the middle of both feet.
The partner calls the colour of one marker.
The player takes one controlled step towards that marker while maintaining balance and visual contact with the football.
The player returns immediately to the middle and resets the stance.
The partner then raises, lowers or moves the football slightly to test whether the player can remain ready without standing upright.
Complete six to eight calls before changing roles.
Award one point whenever the player moves and resets without crossing the feet, losing balance or looking away from the football.
coachingPoints: Keep the feet wide enough to create stability but not so wide that movement becomes restricted.
Flex through the ankles, knees and hips rather than bending only at the waist.
Keep the chest lifted and eyes directed towards the football.
Hold the hands comfortably in front of the body, ready to protect or reach.
Distribute weight through the middle of both feet rather than sitting on the heels.
Use short first steps and avoid crossing the feet during initial movement.
Return to the same balanced position after every movement.
Maintain relaxed shoulders and hands.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player can hold the stance without rocking forwards or backwards.
The relationship between foot width, knee bend and body control.
Whether the player watches the football while responding to the colour call.
Whether the first step is short, balanced and appropriate to the direction.
Whether the player returns to a consistent starting position.
Any excessive knee collapse, heel loading or waist bending.

commonErrors.error: Player stands too upright.
commonErrors.correction: Ask the player to soften the ankles, knees and hips while keeping the chest lifted.

commonErrors.error: Feet are positioned too close together.
commonErrors.correction: Widen the base until the player can resist a light shoulder tap without stepping.

commonErrors.error: Weight is held on the heels.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage the player to feel pressure through the middle and front half of both feet.

commonErrors.error: Player bends forward at the waist.
commonErrors.correction: Lift the chest and lower the body by flexing the knees and hips.

commonErrors.error: Feet cross during lateral movement.
commonErrors.correction: Use one short directional step and then recover to the starting base.

progressions: Increase the speed and unpredictability of the colour calls.
Call two colours in sequence before the player resets.
Add a small vertical jump after each directional step.
Replace colour calls with movements of the football.
Introduce a second player mirroring the working player without contact.
regressions: Remove the directional movement and practise holding the stance.
Use only forward and backward calls.
Allow the player to look at the marker before moving.
Reduce the working square to limit movement distance.
successIndicators: Establish a stable stance without repeated adjustment.
Keep their eyes on the football.
Move in any direction without crossing the feet.
Maintain chest position and knee flexion.
Return quickly to a balanced ready position.
matchApplication: A stable stance gives the ruck the ability to react to an umpire’s throw-up or boundary throw-in, adjust to an opponent’s position and move into the contest without losing balance. It also provides the foundation for safe jumping, body positioning and follow-up work.
relatedDrills: SP-080 – Spoiling and Aerial Defence Chapter Final Assessment

title: Controlled Ruck Approach Footwork
primarySkill: Ruck approach footwork
objective: Teach players to use a controlled, balanced approach that places the body in an effective take-off position beneath the ball.
groundSize: A 12 × 5-metre lane for each group.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Create a five-metre-wide lane.
Mark starting points three metres, five metres and seven metres from a central take-off zone.
Place a hoop or four flat markers around the intended take-off position.
One feeder stands beside the take-off zone with a football.
Players form a line at the selected starting marker.
No opposing ruck is used.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder holds the football above the take-off zone to provide a visual target.
The first player begins in the stance established in RK-001.
On the feeder’s call, the player approaches at controlled speed.
The player uses short adjustment steps to arrive balanced inside the take-off zone.
The player reaches upward without jumping, touches the football with an open hand and lands or stops under control.
The player exits to the opposite side of the lane and returns to the end of the line.
After two repetitions, move the starting group to a different approach distance.
Award one point for entering the take-off zone balanced and one point for maintaining visual contact with the football.
coachingPoints: Accelerate smoothly rather than sprinting immediately.
Keep the eyes on the football throughout the approach.
Use shorter steps as the player reaches the contest.
Avoid reaching the take-off area with the feet too close together.
Keep the body tall enough to see the ball while retaining knee flexion.
Arrive underneath or slightly to the preferred side of the football.
Maintain forward momentum without drifting past the contest.
Exit away from the next approaching player.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player changes from longer approach steps to shorter adjustment steps.
Whether the player arrives too quickly and overruns the target area.
The width and balance of the final foot placement.
Whether the chest remains directed towards the football.
Whether the player can approach effectively from different distances.
The player’s awareness when exiting the contest area.

commonErrors.error: Player sprints through the take-off zone.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce approach speed and require two short adjustment steps before reaching.

commonErrors.error: Final steps become long and uncontrolled.
commonErrors.correction: Mark two smaller stepping zones before the take-off area.

commonErrors.error: Player watches the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Require the player to call “ball” while maintaining visual contact.

commonErrors.error: Feet finish too close together.
commonErrors.correction: Use two separate foot markers inside the take-off zone.

commonErrors.error: Player drifts past the football.
commonErrors.correction: Ask the player to stop or land within the marked take-off area.

progressions: Remove the visible take-off hoop.
Toss the football slightly higher so the player must judge the arrival point.
Vary the starting angle rather than approaching only in a straight line.
Add a controlled vertical jump.
Introduce a passive opponent approaching from the opposite side.
regressions: Begin only three metres from the take-off zone.
Use fixed foot markers for the final two steps.
Hold the football stationary rather than tossing it.
successIndicators: Remain underneath the intended contest point.
Keep their eyes on the football throughout the movement.
matchApplication: Effective rucks rarely arrive at every contest from the same distance or angle. Controlled approach footwork allows the player to judge the ball, avoid overrunning the contest and establish a safe, balanced position from which to jump or engage an opponent.
relatedDrills: RK-001 – Balanced Ruck Stance and Ready Position

title: Ball-Flight Leap Timing
primarySkill: Ruck leap timing
objective: Develop the ability to time a vertical leap so the player reaches maximum height as the football enters the tapping zone.
groundSize: One 8 × 8-metre area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a central take-off zone two metres in diameter.
A feeder stands three to four metres away with a football.
The ruck begins four metres from the take-off zone.
A second player retrieves footballs and returns them to the feeder.
Ensure the landing surface is clear, level and dry.
Limit each player to four consecutive jumps before rotating.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder gives a consistent vertical toss into the centre of the take-off zone.
The ruck approaches using controlled footwork.
The player judges the rise of the football and selects the take-off moment.
The player jumps vertically and reaches with an open hand.
The player attempts to touch the lower half of the football at maximum comfortable reach.
The player lands on both feet with flexed knees and holds balance for two seconds.
The retriever collects the football and the group rotates after four attempts.
Score one point for contacting the football near the top of the jump and one point for a controlled landing.
coachingPoints: Read the football from the feeder’s release rather than waiting until it begins to descend.
Use the final step to organise the take-off rather than creating excessive forward momentum.
Jump upward through the hips, knees and ankles.
Extend the tapping arm late enough to avoid reaching maximum extension too early.
Keep the non-tapping arm controlled and away from the face.
Land with knees flexed and feet apart.
Do not continue jumping when technique deteriorates through fatigue.
Adjust the approach rather than leaning or reaching from underneath the body.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The point in the ball flight at which the player begins the jump.
Whether maximum arm extension occurs before, during or after the highest point.
Excessive forward drift through the contest.
Whether the player jumps from a balanced final step.
The position of both feet on landing.
Whether fatigue reduces jump timing or landing control.

commonErrors.error: Player jumps too early.
commonErrors.correction: Delay the take-off until the football is closer to the intended tapping height.

commonErrors.error: Player jumps after the ball has passed the best contact point.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage earlier reading of the feeder’s release.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches fully before leaving the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the arm relaxed until the upward jump has begun.

commonErrors.error: Player travels forward instead of upward.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the approach and focus on a vertical final step.

commonErrors.error: Landing is stiff or narrow.
commonErrors.correction: Land with feet apart and absorb force through the ankles, knees and hips.

progressions: Vary the height of the toss.
Vary the starting distance.
Move the landing point slightly left or right.
Add a passive opposing ruck who jumps beside the player without body contact.
Ask the player to palm the football to a stationary target.
regressions: Begin directly beside the take-off zone.
Use a stationary suspended football or soft target.
Remove the approach and practise take-off and landing only.
successIndicators: Judge the flight from the initial release.
Reach the football close to maximum jump height.
Jump vertically without overrunning the contest.
Land safely and regain balance immediately.
Maintain timing across varying toss heights.
matchApplication: Ruck contests are determined by the relationship between the ball’s flight, the player’s approach and the timing of the leap. Reaching maximum height at the correct moment increases the chance of first contact while reducing unsafe reaching, drifting and late body contact.
relatedDrills: RK-001 – Balanced Ruck Stance and Ready Position
SP-080 – Spoiling and Aerial Defence Chapter Final Assessment

title: Open-Hand Palm Contact
primarySkill: Clean palm contact
objective: Teach players to contact the football cleanly with an open palm and direct it without grabbing, punching or striking dangerously.
groundSize: One 6 × 6-metre area for each group.
equipment: Optional soft footballs for younger players
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Players work in pairs.
One feeder stands two to three metres from the ruck.
Place a hoop or one-metre target square three metres to the ruck’s preferred tapping side.
Begin without an approach or jump.
The feeder uses gentle underarm tosses above the ruck’s reaching shoulder.
Change the target side after each set.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder tosses the football above the ruck’s tapping shoulder.
The ruck tracks the football and presents an open hand with fingers spread naturally.
The player contacts the lower or side panel of the football using the centre of the palm and finger pads.
The wrist and forearm guide the football towards the target.
The player does not catch, carry or punch the football.
Complete eight taps before changing roles.
Score two points when the football lands in the hoop and one point when it passes within one metre.
Repeat with the opposite hand where appropriate.
coachingPoints: Keep the hand open and relaxed before contact.
Present a firm palm without locking the elbow.
Contact the lower half of the football when directing it forward or outward.
Use the wrist and forearm to guide rather than swinging the entire arm.
Watch the football into the hand.
Keep the fingers away from the opponent’s face in later contested work.
Finish the palm towards the target.
Practise both hands while recognising each player’s preferred side.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Which part of the hand contacts the football.
Whether the player closes the fingers and attempts to catch.
The relationship between contact point and intended direction.
Excessive arm swinging or elbow locking.
Whether the player watches the football through contact.
The difference between preferred-hand and non-preferred-hand control.

commonErrors.error: Player punches the football with a closed fist.
commonErrors.correction: Open the hand and use the palm and finger pads to redirect the ball.

commonErrors.error: Fingers close around the football.
commonErrors.correction: Practise quick touch-and-release contacts with no holding time.

commonErrors.error: Contact occurs on top of the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Reach underneath or to the side of the football according to the target.

commonErrors.error: Arm swings across the body.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the elbow underneath the hand and finish directly towards the target.

commonErrors.error: Player looks at the target before contact.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain vision on the football until it has left the hand.

progressions: Add a controlled vertical jump.
Increase the height and speed of the toss.
Use smaller target zones.
Alternate targets immediately before the toss.
Introduce a passive opposing hand competing for the football.
regressions: Hold the football above the player’s head for stationary contact.
Remove scoring and focus only on hand shape.
successIndicators: Contact the football with an open hand.
Direct the ball towards the intended side.
Reproduce the hand shape with either hand.
matchApplication: Clean palm contact allows the ruck to give midfielders a controllable opportunity rather than creating an unpredictable loose ball. Safe hand presentation also reduces the likelihood of illegal or dangerous contact in an opposed ruck contest.
relatedDrills: RK-001 – Balanced Ruck Stance and Ready Position

title: Four-Zone Hit Direction
primarySkill: Directional hit-zone control
objective: Develop the ability to direct a ruck tap towards four basic hit zones in response to a clear visual or verbal cue.
groundSize: A 10 × 10-metre square.
equipment: Four different-coloured hoops or cone gates
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Place four target zones three metres from the contest: front, back, left and right.
Assign a different colour to each zone.
One feeder stands outside the working area.
One ruck begins at the central point.
One retriever rotates between the target zones.
The feeder holds coloured cards or calls the target colour.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder presents the target colour immediately before tossing the football.
The ruck identifies the corresponding hit zone.
The feeder tosses the football vertically over the central point.
The ruck uses an open palm to direct the football towards the called zone.
The retriever collects the football and returns it to the feeder.
The player completes eight taps, with the target changing each time.
Award two points when the football lands in the target and one point when it lands within one metre.
Rotate the ruck, feeder and retriever roles.
coachingPoints: Scan and identify the target before focusing completely on the football.
Adjust hand position according to the required direction.
Contact underneath the football for forward or higher taps.
Contact the side panel when directing the ball laterally.
Use controlled wrist action rather than excessive force.
Keep the body balanced through contact.
Do not sacrifice clean contact by trying to hit the football too hard.
Reset the stance after each repetition.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player processes the target cue before the toss.
The accuracy difference between front, back and lateral taps.
Whether the body rotates excessively during lateral direction.
Whether force is appropriate for the target distance.
The player’s ability to reset between repetitions.

commonErrors.error: Every tap travels in the same direction.
commonErrors.correction: Change the hand position and contact point to match the called zone.

commonErrors.error: Player uses excessive force.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the target distance and prioritise landing accuracy.

commonErrors.error: Player turns away from the football.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the chest mostly square and guide the ball with the hand and wrist.

commonErrors.error: Target cue is forgotten after the toss.
commonErrors.correction: Require the player to call the target colour aloud before contact.

commonErrors.error: Backward taps travel too high or short.
commonErrors.correction: Contact the front-lower panel and finish the palm behind the body line.

progressions: Reveal the target after the football has been tossed.
Reduce the size of each target.
Add a controlled approach and jump.
Position a midfielder inside each target as a moving receiver.
Introduce a passive opposing ruck.
regressions: Keep the target constant for four repetitions.
Move the targets closer to the contest.
successIndicators: Change the hand and contact angle appropriately.
Deliver controllable taps to all four areas.
Maintain clean technique while making a decision.
Use suitable force for the target distance.
matchApplication: Ruck craft requires more than winning contact. Directing the ball towards a planned space allows midfielders to start from predictable positions, create separation from opponents and execute a coordinated stoppage exit.

title: Front-Position Ruck Bodywork
primarySkill: Safe front-position bodywork
objective: Teach players to establish and maintain front position using balanced footwork and legal body contact without holding, blocking dangerously or turning away from the football.
groundSize: One 5 × 5-metre contest square per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a 5 × 5-metre square.
Two rucks begin side by side, one metre apart.
A feeder stands four metres away.
Identify one player as the position player and the other as the pressure player.
Contact is limited to shoulder, side and hip bodywork.
Holding, pushing in the back, high contact and extended-arm blocking are prohibited.
Use a coach-controlled toss that lands inside the square.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both players begin in balanced ruck stances.
The feeder calls “set” and then tosses the football into the square.
The position player uses footwork to move between the opponent and the expected drop point.
The pressure player applies controlled body pressure without tackling or holding.
The position player maintains visual contact with the football and reaches to palm it.
The contest finishes immediately after the tap or if either player loses balance.
Players swap roles after three contests.
Award one point for legally establishing front position and one point for making first contact with the football.
coachingPoints: Win space initially with the feet rather than extended arms.
Keep the hips and shoulders stable when contact occurs.
Maintain a wide, balanced base.
Use the side of the body rather than turning the back into the opponent.
Keep the eyes tracking the football.
Avoid reaching across an opponent’s head or face.
Reposition if the ball flight changes rather than leaning excessively.
Stop the contest immediately when balance or safety is compromised.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether front position is gained through footwork or illegal arm use.
The height and legality of body contact.
Whether players remain balanced and able to jump.
Whether the position player loses sight of the football.
The response when the toss moves away from the expected drop point.
Whether stronger players overpower partners rather than practising technique.

commonErrors.error: Player extends an arm to hold the opponent away.
commonErrors.correction: Bring the arm back inside the body line and use footwork to protect space.

commonErrors.error: Player turns their back fully into the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Use a side-on position that allows vision of both ball and opponent.

commonErrors.error: Feet become narrow during contact.
commonErrors.correction: Reset with a wider base and flexed knees.

commonErrors.error: Player leans and falls through the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce pressure and require balance to be held after the tap.

commonErrors.error: Contact becomes high or forceful.
commonErrors.correction: Stop immediately, lower intensity and reinforce shoulder-to-shoulder or side contact only.

progressions: Allow both players to compete equally for front position.
Vary the toss so players must reposition.
Add a controlled jump after body position is established.
Include a midfielder who collects the winning tap.
Increase pressure gradually while maintaining legal contact.
regressions: Use bump pads instead of player-to-player contact.
Begin with a walking body-position exercise.
successIndicators: Keep a stable base under pressure.
Track the football throughout the contest.
Complete the contest without holding or unsafe movement.
matchApplication: At boundary throw-ins and congested stoppages, rucks must often create access to the ball before jumping. Safe front-position bodywork allows the ruck to protect a preferred line, limit the opponent’s approach and remain capable of making a controlled tap.
relatedDrills: RK-001 – Balanced Ruck Stance and Ready Position

title: Tap-and-Follow Ground Ball
primarySkill: Ruck follow-up after the tap
objective: Develop the habit of landing, locating the football and contributing immediately to the next phase rather than remaining outside the contest.
groundSize: A 12 × 10-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Place two exit gates four metres away on opposite sides.
One feeder, one ruck, one midfielder and one shadow defender work in each repetition.
The defender begins one metre behind the midfielder.
The feeder tosses the ball to the ruck.
The ruck intentionally directs the ball into a marked ground-ball zone two metres away.
Pressure remains at shadow intensity.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder tosses the football to the ruck.
The ruck palms the ball into the ground-ball zone.
Immediately after landing, the ruck turns, locates the ball and moves to support.
The midfielder attempts to collect the football while the defender applies shadow pressure.
The midfielder may handball to the ruck if the ruck presents in support.
The ruck or midfielder carries the ball through either exit gate.
The repetition ends when the ball exits, is fumbled outside the area or the defender intercepts.
Rotate feeder, ruck, midfielder and defender roles.
Award one point for a controlled tap and one point for a successful follow-up involvement.
coachingPoints: Land with balance before accelerating to the next contest.
Locate the football immediately rather than watching the original tap.
Move towards the ball or into a useful support lane.
Keep the hands ready to receive.
Communicate whether the ruck is supporting inside, outside or behind.
Avoid following the same line as the midfielder and creating congestion.
Use a quick handball or block only when legal and appropriate.
Treat the tap as the beginning of the play, not the completion of the role.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How quickly the ruck regains balance after landing.
Whether the ruck immediately locates the ball.
The quality of the support angle.
Whether the ruck becomes stationary after the tap.
Communication between the ruck and midfielder.
Whether the midfielder uses the ruck as a genuine option.
The quality of disposal under shadow pressure.

commonErrors.error: Ruck remains at the original contest point.
commonErrors.correction: Require the ruck to move within one second of landing.

commonErrors.error: Ruck runs directly behind the midfielder.
commonErrors.correction: Create a separate inside or outside support lane.

commonErrors.error: Player watches the tap instead of locating the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Turn the head and shoulders immediately after landing.

commonErrors.error: Follow-up movement is rushed and unbalanced.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the landing before accelerating.

commonErrors.error: Midfielder ignores the supporting ruck.
commonErrors.correction: Award the second point only when the support option is recognised or used.

progressions: Increase the defender to controlled pressure.
Add a second midfielder and second defender.
Allow the tap to travel to different ground-ball zones.
Add a turnover transition if the defender wins possession.
Require a second disposal before exiting the area.
regressions: Allow the ruck to begin on the ground without jumping.
Roll the football into the ground-ball zone instead of tapping it.
successIndicators: Contribute to the clearance rather than standing outside the play.
matchApplication: Modern rucks are expected to remain involved after the initial aerial contest. A quick follow-up can create an extra number at ground level, protect the ball carrier, receive a release handball or prevent the opposition from escaping the stoppage.

title: Ruck-to-Midfielder Call System
primarySkill: Ruck and midfielder communication
objective: Establish a simple communication system that allows a ruck and midfielder to agree on a hit zone before the contest and execute the plan together.
groundSize: One 10 × 10-metre stoppage area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark four hit zones around a central ruck point.
One ruck begins at the contest.
One midfielder begins three metres away.
One feeder holds the football.
Use four agreed calls, such as “front”, “back”, “left” and “right”.
The midfielder must begin from a neutral position rather than standing inside the target zone.
Groups rotate through all three roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
Before the toss, the ruck scans the target zones and makes eye contact with the midfielder.
The ruck or midfielder communicates the planned hit zone using the agreed call.
The feeder waits until both players confirm readiness.
The feeder tosses the football vertically.
The ruck directs the tap towards the nominated zone.
The midfielder delays movement, then accelerates into the zone to receive the football.
The midfielder collects and handballs back to the feeder.
Repeat six times before rotating roles.
Award one point for clear communication and one point for a successful connection in the nominated zone.
coachingPoints: Use short, consistent calls that all players understand.
Make eye contact before communicating.
Ensure both ruck and midfielder acknowledge the call.
Do not reveal the intended movement too early through body position.
The midfielder should move late enough to preserve space.
The ruck must still judge the football rather than blindly tapping to a call.
Reset and recommunicate when the feeder changes the starting conditions.
Use voice volume appropriate to the training environment.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether communication occurs early enough to be useful.
Whether both players interpret the call identically.
The timing of the midfielder’s movement.
Whether the ruck’s body position gives away the plan.
Accuracy of the tap into the nominated space.
Whether players reset after a failed connection.
The clarity and volume of the calls.

commonErrors.error: Ruck and midfielder use different terminology.
commonErrors.correction: Establish one shared set of calls before restarting.

commonErrors.error: Midfielder moves before the football is tossed.
commonErrors.correction: Require the midfielder to hold the starting position until the feeder releases the ball.

commonErrors.error: Call is too late.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and acknowledge the plan before the feeder begins.

commonErrors.error: Ruck stares at the target zone.
commonErrors.correction: Scan briefly, then return vision to the football.

commonErrors.error: Players stop communicating after a mistake.
commonErrors.correction: Reset immediately and confirm the next call clearly.

progressions: Allow the feeder to cancel the original call and force a late change.
Add a passive opposition midfielder.
Use disguised hand signals instead of voice.
Add a second midfielder running to a decoy zone.
Introduce a passive opposing ruck.
regressions: Use only front and back calls.
Keep the same target for three repetitions.
Allow the midfielder to start closer to the zone.
Use stationary palm contacts without a jump.
successIndicators: Time the midfielder’s movement with the tap.
matchApplication: Clear pre-stoppage communication allows the ruck and midfielders to operate as a coordinated unit. Shared calls improve hit-zone understanding, reduce hesitation and give the receiver a better chance of arriving in space at the same time as the football.

title: Basic Stoppage Starting Positions
primarySkill: Stoppage positioning
objective: Teach a ruck and three midfielders to organise balanced starting positions that provide attacking options while maintaining defensive coverage.
groundSize: A 15 × 15-metre stoppage area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Place three midfield starting markers around the contest: inside, outside and defensive.
Position one ruck at the central point.
Use one feeder and three midfielders.
Mark four potential hit zones.
No opposition is used initially.
Each midfielder is assigned a clear responsibility before the repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The group organises into the ruck, inside midfielder, outside midfielder and defensive midfielder roles.
Before the toss, all players scan the available space and confirm the intended hit zone.
The feeder calls “live” and tosses the football.
The ruck taps towards the nominated zone.
The designated receiver moves to the ball.
The other midfielders hold spacing, provide support or protect the defensive side.
The receiver collects and completes a handball to one supporting teammate.
The group exits through a marked gate.
After each repetition, players rotate midfield roles.
Award one point for correct starting structure and one point for a clean exit.
coachingPoints: Avoid placing all midfielders on the same side of the stoppage.
Maintain enough width for players to accelerate into the contest.
Give each midfielder a primary and secondary responsibility.
Keep one player capable of responding if the opposition wins the tap.
Align the starting structure with the nominated hit zone.
Do not crowd the ruck’s approach or landing space.
Scan before taking the starting position.
Adjust positions to the available space rather than standing on fixed marks without thought.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ruck has a clear approach and landing area.
Whether every player understands their role.
Whether the non-receiving midfielders remain connected to the play.
Defensive coverage behind the intended hit zone.
Whether players adjust to different nominated zones.
The timing and angle of support after possession is won.

commonErrors.error: All midfielders start close to the football.
commonErrors.correction: Restore inside, outside and defensive spacing before restarting.

commonErrors.error: Players stand on the same side of the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Rebalance the structure to provide multiple hit zones.

commonErrors.error: Non-receivers become spectators.
commonErrors.correction: Assign every player a support or defensive responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Midfielder blocks the ruck’s movement.
commonErrors.correction: Move starting positions away from the ruck’s approach and landing line.

commonErrors.error: Structure remains unchanged for every hit zone.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the starting shape to match the intended tap direction.

progressions: Add three passive opposition midfielders.
Allow the feeder to change the hit-zone call.
Include a turnover exit for the opposition.
Remove positional markers.
Begin from different stoppage locations, including boundary-side and centre-square positions.
regressions: Walk through each role before adding the toss.
Predetermine the receiver and exit gate.
successIndicators: Leave a clear ruck contest area.
Adjust structure to the intended hit zone.
Support the receiver after the tap.
matchApplication: Effective stoppage play begins before the ball enters the air. Balanced starting positions give the ruck multiple hit options, help midfielders enter the contest at speed and provide protection if the opposition wins possession.

title: Three-Player Ruck-to-Clearance Connection
primarySkill: Basic ruck-to-clearance connection
objective: Combine fundamental ruck technique, communication, midfielder movement and support play to produce a controlled two-disposal clearance from a basic stoppage.
groundSize: A 20 × 15-metre area with two five-metre-wide exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central stoppage point.
Place four hit-zone markers around the contest.
Create two exit gates 10 metres away.
Each attacking group contains one ruck and two midfielders.
Add one shadow defender who begins behind the receiving midfielder.
One feeder controls the toss.
The ruck and midfielders agree on the hit zone before each repetition.
The two midfielders begin in separate inside and outside positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ruck and midfielders scan the area and communicate the intended hit zone.
The feeder waits until all players are organised and then calls “live”.
The feeder tosses the football vertically.
The ruck approaches or jumps and attempts to direct the ball into the nominated zone.
The receiving midfielder times movement to collect the tap.
The shadow defender applies controlled pressure without tackling.
The second midfielder moves into a supporting lane.
The receiver handballs to the support player.
The support player exits through either gate.
The ruck lands, follows the play and provides an additional support option.
If the defender intercepts or forces a fumble, the defender exits through the opposite gate.
Rotate all roles after three repetitions.
Award one point for a successful tap connection, one point for the support handball and one point for a controlled exit.
coachingPoints: Establish the plan before the toss but remain capable of reacting to an imperfect ball.
The receiver should move late and at speed.
Direct the tap into space rather than directly onto a stationary player.
The support midfielder must hold width until the receiver gains possession.
Use voice and visual communication throughout the sequence.
The ruck should follow the play after landing.
Protect the inside of the stoppage if the tap misses the intended target.
Take the most appropriate exit rather than forcing the originally preferred gate.
Maintain disposal quality under pressure.
Reset quickly after a turnover or failed connection.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ruck delivers to the nominated space.
The receiver’s starting position and movement timing.
The support midfielder’s width and angle.
Whether the ruck contributes after landing.
Decision making when the tap is imperfect.
The speed of transition after a turnover.
Whether players crowd the same exit lane.

commonErrors.error: Receiver moves before the toss and fills the hit zone early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the starting position and accelerate after the feeder releases the football.

commonErrors.error: Support midfielder collapses onto the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain width and present a clear release lane.

commonErrors.error: Ruck stops after the tap.
commonErrors.correction: Require immediate follow-up towards the clearance line.

commonErrors.error: Players force the planned exit despite pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Scan both gates and use the safer available option.

commonErrors.error: Tap is directed at the receiver’s body.
commonErrors.correction: Tap into the space the midfielder is moving towards.

commonErrors.error: Poor tap causes the whole group to stop.
commonErrors.correction: Continue playing and react to the loose football until the repetition ends.

progressions: Increase the defender to controlled tackling pressure.
Add a second defender against the support midfielder.
Allow the ruck to select the hit zone after reading the defensive setup.
Remove visible target markers.
Start from a boundary throw-in position.
Require the clearance to finish with a kick to a leading target.
Add a five-second time limit to exit the area.
regressions: Predetermine the hit zone and exit gate.
Allow the receiver to begin closer to the target area.
Use a stationary palm instead of a jump.
Walk through the complete sequence before increasing speed.
successIndicators: Connect the ruck tap with a moving midfielder.
Maintain useful spacing between receiver and support player.
Use the ruck as a follow-up option.
Adapt when the football does not travel perfectly.
Exit through the most appropriate gate.
matchApplication: The drill replicates the fundamental components of a stoppage clearance: an agreed hit zone, a midfielder arriving at speed, a supporting disposal option and the ruck following the play. These connections allow a team to move the football away from congestion while retaining protection against an opposition win.

title: Boundary Throw-In Body Position
primarySkill: Boundary throw-in positioning
objective: Develop a balanced starting position and curved approach that allows the ruck to track a boundary throw-in while protecting space and remaining capable of tapping to either side.
groundSize: A 12 × 10-metre area positioned beside a marked boundary line.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a straight boundary line approximately 12 metres long.
Position a feeder outside the boundary with several footballs.
Mark a central landing zone three metres inside the boundary.
Place one hit-zone gate towards the corridor side and another towards the boundary side.
The ruck begins three to five metres from the expected landing zone.
Use only one ruck initially.
Ensure the approach and landing areas are clear.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder simulates a boundary throw-in by delivering the football over their head towards the marked landing zone.
The ruck tracks the flight from release and approaches on a controlled curved line.
The player positions the body side-on enough to see the football while preserving access to both hit zones.
The feeder calls “corridor” or “boundary” as the football reaches the top of its flight.
The ruck jumps and directs the tap towards the nominated gate.
The player lands under control and follows the football for three metres.
Complete six repetitions before rotating roles.
Award one point for correct body position, one point for a controlled tap and one point for a balanced landing.
coachingPoints: Track the football from the feeder’s release.
Approach on a line that allows adjustment if the throw drifts.
Avoid standing directly underneath the expected ball flight too early.
Keep the chest partly open towards the field.
Use short adjustment steps near the landing zone.
Jump vertically rather than drifting across the boundary.
Keep the tapping arm clear of the face and head area.
Land inside the field and move immediately into the follow-up phase.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player judges the throw from the initial release.
The angle and control of the approach.
Whether the player becomes trapped directly underneath the football.
Body orientation relative to the boundary and corridor.
The ability to change tap direction after a late call.
Landing balance and immediate follow-up movement.

commonErrors.error: Player approaches in a straight line and overruns the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Use a curved approach with shorter final steps.

commonErrors.error: Player turns completely towards the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the chest partly open towards the field and hit zones.

commonErrors.error: Player stands under the football too early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold depth and move into the drop zone as the ball descends.

commonErrors.error: Tap repeatedly travels over the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Contact the outer panel and finish the palm back towards the field.

commonErrors.error: Player lands and remains stationary.
commonErrors.correction: Require immediate movement towards the tap after landing.

progressions: Vary the height and depth of the throw.
Remove the verbal target call and use a midfielder’s movement as the cue.
Add a passive opposing ruck.
Add one midfielder at each hit-zone gate.
Allow full controlled ruck competition.
regressions: Walk through the approach without jumping.
Use a gentle underarm toss from inside the boundary.
successIndicators: Arrive balanced at the correct depth.
Maintain access to both hit zones.
Direct the football back into play.
Land safely and follow the tap.
matchApplication: Boundary throw-ins require the ruck to judge a less predictable ball flight while operating close to the line. Correct body orientation and approach depth help the player keep the football in play, access midfield support and avoid being trapped underneath the contest.

title: Centre Bounce Take-Off Line
primarySkill: Centre-bounce approach alignment
objective: Teach the ruck to select and maintain a controlled approach line that creates a balanced take-off position at a centre-bounce-style contest.
groundSize: A 15 × 8-metre lane with a central contest circle.
equipment: Optional soft landing mats for introductory work
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a three-metre-diameter central contest circle.
Create two approach lanes entering the circle from opposite sides.
Place starting markers five and seven metres from the centre.
Position one feeder beside the circle.
One player performs the approach while another retrieves.
Begin without an opposing ruck.
Mark a safe landing zone beyond the take-off point.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ruck begins at the nominated starting marker.
The feeder gives a vertical toss into the central contest area.
The ruck accelerates along the approach lane while tracking the football.
The player uses adjustment steps to select a take-off point before reaching the centre.
The ruck jumps vertically, touches or palms the football and lands beyond the take-off point.
The player exits through the far side of the circle.
Vary the toss slightly left, right, short and deep.
Complete four approaches from each starting distance before rotating.
Score one point for maintaining the approach line and one point for taking off under control.
coachingPoints: Begin from a stance that permits immediate forward movement.
Build speed gradually rather than sprinting from the first step.
Track the football while maintaining awareness of the contest circle.
Shorten the final steps when the toss changes.
Take off before moving underneath the football.
Jump upward through the body rather than reaching from behind.
Keep the landing path clear.
Exit the contest quickly after landing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player stays within the approach lane.
The relationship between approach speed and take-off control.
Whether the final steps adjust to changes in the toss.
The player’s take-off distance from the centre.
Landing position and awareness after contact.

commonErrors.error: Player sprints too quickly and cannot adjust.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the initial speed and build gradually towards the contest.

commonErrors.error: Take-off occurs directly underneath the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Begin the jump earlier and reach forward at maximum height.

commonErrors.error: Player changes line sharply at the final moment.
commonErrors.correction: Read the toss earlier and make smaller progressive adjustments.

commonErrors.error: Final step is excessively long.
commonErrors.correction: Use two short organising steps before take-off.

commonErrors.error: Player lands across the neighbouring approach lane.
commonErrors.correction: Jump and land within the same controlled movement corridor.

progressions: Add a passive ruck approaching from the opposite side.
Vary the starting distance without warning.
Add a directional tap target.
Introduce controlled shoulder-to-shoulder contest pressure.
Add midfielders moving to nominated hit zones.
regressions: Start three metres from the contest.
Keep every toss at the same height and position.
successIndicators: Adjust the final steps to the football.
Take off before moving underneath the contest.
Exit without interfering with another player’s path.
matchApplication: Centre-bounce ruck contests place both players on converging approach lines. A controlled line improves the chance of reaching the football at maximum height while reducing late adjustments, excessive body contact and unsafe landing positions.
relatedDrills: RK-001 – Balanced Ruck Stance and Ready Position

title: Stationary Opposed Palm Contest
primarySkill: Opposed ruck contact
objective: Introduce controlled opposition while teaching players to compete for first contact without using an approach, excessive force or unsafe arm movement.
groundSize: One 5 × 5-metre contest area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central contest point.
Position two rucks on opposite sides, approximately one metre apart.
Both players begin stationary.
One feeder stands three metres away.
Place one target hoop on each side of the contest.
Assign each ruck a different target.
Prohibit run-ups, holding, extended-arm blocks and high contact.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both rucks establish balanced starting stances.
The feeder gives a gentle vertical toss between the players.
Both players compete for first contact using an open hand.
Each ruck attempts to direct the football towards their assigned target.
Players may use controlled side-to-side body pressure but may not displace the opponent with an extended arm.
The contest ends after the first clear tap.
Complete four contests before changing target sides.
Rotate one player with the feeder after eight contests.
Award one point for first legal contact and one point for directing the ball towards the target.
coachingPoints: Maintain an open hand and safe arm path.
Keep the eyes on the football rather than the opponent’s hand.
Establish balance before the toss.
Use body position without holding or pushing.
Reach at the top of the jump.
Protect personal space with posture rather than swinging the non-tapping arm.
Continue through the landing safely.
Match players appropriately for size, experience and confidence.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the players remain focused on the football.
The legality and safety of arm movement.
Whether stronger players rely on force instead of technique.
The direction and control of the winning tap.

commonErrors.error: Player watches the opponent rather than the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Return vision to the football and compete through timing.

commonErrors.error: Non-tapping arm swings across the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the arm bent and close to the body.

commonErrors.error: Player pushes before the toss.
commonErrors.correction: Reset with no contact until the football is released.

commonErrors.error: Tap is made with a closed fist.
commonErrors.correction: Present an open palm and guide the football.

commonErrors.error: Players collide because the contest is too intense.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce jump height, match players appropriately and restore controlled pressure.

progressions: Add one controlled approach step.
Allow players to select either target.
Add midfielders to collect the tap.
Vary the height of the toss.
Progress to a full controlled ruck approach.
regressions: Remove jumping and use standing reaches.
Allow one player to be passive.
Increase the starting distance between players.
successIndicators: Maintain safe hand and arm positions.
Use timing rather than excessive force.
Direct the football towards the assigned target.
matchApplication: Rucks must compete against an opponent while continuing to track the football and use legal technique. Controlled stationary contests introduce opposition without the speed and collision demands of a full centre bounce or boundary throw-in.

title: Non-Preferred-Hand Hit Zones
primarySkill: Non-preferred-hand ruck tapping
objective: Develop functional tapping ability with the non-preferred hand so the ruck can access hit zones that are unavailable with the preferred hand.
groundSize: One 8 × 8-metre area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Position one ruck at a central marker.
Place four target hoops two to three metres away.
One feeder stands in front of the ruck.
Identify the player’s preferred and non-preferred tapping hands.
The first set uses only the non-preferred hand.
Use gentle vertical or shoulder-height tosses.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder displays or calls a target colour.
The feeder tosses the football towards the ruck’s non-preferred-hand side.
The player presents an open hand and directs the football towards the called target.
The player remains stationary for the first four repetitions.
The next four repetitions include a small vertical jump.
Complete eight to twelve taps before changing roles.
Award two points for landing inside the target and one point for landing within one metre.
Compare accuracy with the preferred hand without allowing the preferred hand to dominate the session.
coachingPoints: Establish the same open-hand shape used with the preferred hand.
Keep the wrist firm but not locked.
Position the body underneath the non-preferred shoulder.
Avoid reaching across the face with the opposite arm.
Use controlled touch before adding force.
Watch the football onto the palm.
Finish the hand towards the target.
Accept reduced power while building coordination and accuracy.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Differences in hand shape between preferred and non-preferred sides.
Whether the player rotates excessively to access the football.
Whether the player attempts to switch hands late.

commonErrors.error: Player switches to the preferred hand.
commonErrors.correction: Position the toss clearly on the non-preferred side and reinforce the task constraint.

commonErrors.error: Non-preferred hand closes around the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Practise rapid touch-and-release contacts with fingers spread.

commonErrors.error: Player rotates the entire body.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the chest stable and reach through the shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Tap lacks direction.
commonErrors.correction: Finish the palm directly towards the target.

commonErrors.error: Player becomes frustrated by lower accuracy.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce target distance and prioritise clean contact.

progressions: Increase the toss height.
Add a controlled approach.
Use late target calls.
Add a passive opposing ruck on the preferred-hand side.
Alternate preferred and non-preferred hands unpredictably.
regressions: Hold the football stationary above the player.
Remove the jump and decision cue.
successIndicators: Use the non-preferred hand without switching.
Maintain an open and controlled palm.
Direct the football towards multiple targets.
matchApplication: The position of an opponent, the ball flight and the planned hit zone may prevent a ruck from using the preferred hand. Competence on both sides expands the available tactical options and reduces predictable tapping patterns.

title: Tap Weight and Distance Control
primarySkill: Tap force control
objective: Teach players to vary the weight of a ruck tap so the football reaches short, medium and long hit zones at a controllable speed.
groundSize: A 12 × 10-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark one central ruck point.
Create short, medium and long target zones at approximately two, four and six metres.
One feeder stands three metres from the ruck.
One receiver begins behind the target zones.
Assign each zone a colour.
Start with stationary taps before adding a jump.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder calls or displays a target colour.
The receiver moves towards the corresponding zone.
The feeder tosses the football above the ruck.
The ruck varies the force and angle of the palm to deliver the football into the receiver’s path.
The receiver attempts to collect without stopping or reaching backwards.
Complete nine repetitions, with three attempts to each distance.
Rotate ruck, feeder and receiver roles.
Award one point when the ball lands in the zone and an additional point when the receiver collects in stride.
coachingPoints: Match the force of the tap to the distance of the target.
Use touch and wrist control for short targets.
Use a stronger forearm finish for longer targets without punching.
Direct the ball into the receiver’s movement path.
Maintain the same preparation so the tap distance is not obvious.
Prioritise controllability over maximum distance.
Watch the ball through contact.
Adjust for the height and momentum of the toss.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether every tap is struck with the same force.
The relationship between target distance and contact angle.
Whether short taps drop softly into space.
The receiver’s ability to maintain running speed.
The player’s control when changing distances consecutively.

commonErrors.error: Every tap travels to the long zone.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the arm swing and use a softer wrist finish for short targets.

commonErrors.error: Short tap falls directly under the ruck.
commonErrors.correction: Contact the lower panel and guide the football slightly forward.

commonErrors.error: Long tap becomes a punch.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the hand open and increase forearm speed without closing the fist.

commonErrors.error: Receiver must stop to collect.
commonErrors.correction: Tap into the player’s running path rather than current position.

commonErrors.error: Preparation reveals the intended distance.
commonErrors.correction: Use the same stance and approach before changing only the contact finish.

progressions: Call the target after the toss.
Add different target angles.
Introduce a passive opposing midfielder.
Add a controlled jump and approach.
Allow the receiver to choose the target with movement.
regressions: Use only short and medium targets.
Keep the target constant for three repetitions.
successIndicators: Deliver the football at a collectable speed.
Hide the intended tap weight until contact.
matchApplication: Not every stoppage requires the same type of hit. A short drop can bring an inside midfielder into the contest, while a longer tap may release an outside runner. Accurate weight control helps the ruck match the delivery to the team’s structure.

title: Changing Ball-Flight Adjustment
primarySkill: Ruck adjustment to variable ball flight
objective: Develop the ability to adjust footwork, take-off point and tapping hand when the football does not travel to the expected contest position.
groundSize: A 10 × 10-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central expected landing zone.
Place four adjustment zones one metre forward, backward, left and right of centre.
Create two tap targets on opposite sides.
One feeder stands four metres away.
The ruck begins four metres from the central zone.
The feeder deliberately varies toss direction within a safe range.
One retriever returns footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ruck begins the approach expecting the football to land in the central zone.
The feeder tosses the football into one of the five possible landing zones.
The player tracks the flight and adjusts with short steps.
The ruck decides whether to jump, remain grounded or use a different hand.
The player directs the tap towards the nearest available target gate.
The ruck lands or regains balance and follows the football.
Complete eight repetitions before rotating.
Award one point for arriving balanced and one point for selecting an appropriate hand and target.
coachingPoints: Read the release rather than assuming every toss will be perfect.
Keep the approach speed low enough to permit adjustment.
Use several small steps instead of one large sideways lunge.
Do not jump when remaining grounded provides better control.
Select the hand that gives the safest and clearest access.
Maintain balance before attempting direction.
Avoid reaching across the body or face.
Continue the play after an imperfect contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How early the player recognises a changing ball flight.
Whether the approach speed permits adjustment.
The size and control of corrective steps.
The decision to jump or remain grounded.
Hand selection relative to ball position.
Balance and follow-up after an imperfect contest.

commonErrors.error: Player continues towards the original landing point.
commonErrors.correction: Track the football from release and adjust immediately.

commonErrors.error: Player takes one large lateral lunge.
commonErrors.correction: Use multiple short steps to reposition the base.

commonErrors.error: Player jumps when the ball is too low.
commonErrors.correction: Remain grounded and use a controlled standing palm.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches across the body.
commonErrors.correction: Move the feet or select the hand closest to the football.

commonErrors.error: Player gives up when the toss is imperfect.
commonErrors.correction: Continue competing and direct the best available tap.

progressions: Increase the range of safe variation.
Add a late target call.
Introduce a passive opponent.
Add moving midfield receivers.
Progress to variable boundary throw-ins.
regressions: Use only left and right variation.
Announce the landing zone before the toss.
successIndicators: Read changes in ball flight early.
Produce a useful outcome from imperfect delivery.
matchApplication: Umpire throw-ups, boundary throw-ins and centre bounces do not always enter the expected space. Rucks who adjust without losing balance can remain competitive and prevent an imperfect ball flight from automatically favouring the opponent.

title: Defensive Ruck Neutralisation
primarySkill: Neutralising an opposition ruck advantage
objective: Teach the ruck to recognise when clean possession is unlikely and neutralise the contest safely by directing the football into a controlled, defensible area.
groundSize: A 10 × 10-metre contest area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Place two opposition hit-zone gates on one side.
Mark a two-metre defensive neutralisation zone close to the contest.
One attacking ruck is assigned a preferred target.
One defending ruck attempts to deny that target.
One feeder delivers the football.
One midfielder stands behind each target as a collector.
Contact is controlled and matched appropriately.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking ruck is shown the nominated hit zone.
The defending ruck identifies the likely attacking hand and body position.
The feeder tosses the football.
The attacking ruck attempts to deliver a clean tap to the nominated midfielder.
The defending ruck attempts first to win the ball and, if unable, redirects or deadens it into the defensive neutralisation zone.
Both rucks land and follow the football.
The nearest midfielder collects and handballs through an exit gate.
Rotate attacking and defending roles after four contests.
Award the defender one point for preventing the planned hit and an additional point for directing the ball into the neutralisation zone.
coachingPoints: Read the opponent’s stance, hand preference and target alignment.
Compete for the football rather than focusing only on body contact.
Use legal position to reduce access to the preferred hit zone.
When clean control is unavailable, keep the football close and predictable.
Avoid blindly striking the ball into open opposition space.
Maintain an open hand and safe arm action.
Land ready to apply ground-level pressure.
Communicate the neutralised ball to teammates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defender reads the attacking setup before the toss.
Whether contact remains legal and controlled.
The decision between winning, redirecting and deadening the tap.
Immediate follow-up pressure from both rucks.
Whether the defender accidentally creates an opposition clearance.

commonErrors.error: Defender focuses only on blocking the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Return attention to the football and compete through position and timing.

commonErrors.error: Neutralising tap travels into open space.
commonErrors.correction: Soften the hand and direct the ball close to the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender swings across the opponent’s arm.
commonErrors.correction: Use a safe vertical reach and legal body position.

commonErrors.error: Player tries to win every contest cleanly.
commonErrors.correction: Recognise when denial and a close neutral ball are the better outcome.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Land and move immediately towards the football.

progressions: Allow the attacking ruck to choose between two targets.
Add opposition midfield movement.
Remove the visible neutralisation zone.
Add a clearance contest after the tap.
Begin from boundary throw-in and centre-bounce positions.
regressions: Predetermine the attacking hand and target.
Practise deadening the football from stationary tosses.
successIndicators: Keep neutralised taps close and defensible.
matchApplication: When an opponent has superior position or timing, attempting an ambitious attacking tap can create a damaging clearance. A controlled neutralisation keeps the football near the contest, allows teammates to pressure the next possession and limits clean opposition movement.
relatedDrills: RK-015 – Tap Weight and Distance Control

title: Follow-Up Block and Release
primarySkill: Ruck follow-up body positioning
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to recover from the aerial contest, establish a legal body position and create a safe release path for a teammate.
groundSize: A 15 × 12-metre area with two exit gates.
equipment: Optional bump pads for introductory work
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Position one ruck, one attacking midfielder and one defender around the contest.
Add one feeder and one support player.
Create two exit gates eight metres from the stoppage.
The defender begins one metre from the midfielder.
Contact is limited to legal body positioning and controlled shepherding.
No tackling is used initially.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder tosses the football to the ruck.
The ruck taps towards the attacking midfielder.
The ruck lands, locates the defender and moves into a legal body position.
The midfielder collects and chooses an exit gate.
The ruck uses a stationary or moving shepherd to protect the ball carrier’s release path.
The midfielder handballs to the support player or carries through the gate.
If the defender moves around the shepherd, the ruck releases and becomes a receiving option.
If possession is lost, all players transition immediately.
Rotate roles every three repetitions.
Award one point for a legal block and one point for a successful exit.
coachingPoints: Regain balance before engaging another player.
Keep the eyes moving between the football, teammate and defender.
Establish body position without holding or extending the arms.
Keep feet active so the defender cannot move around easily.
Avoid moving into the defender’s path late or dangerously.
Release the shepherd when the teammate has cleared the area.
Become a handball option after the block.
Transition defensively if the opposition wins possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The ruck’s balance immediately after landing.
Whether the defender is located before body contact.
The distance between the shepherd and ball carrier.
Whether the ruck releases at the appropriate time.

commonErrors.error: Ruck charges blindly into the defender.
commonErrors.correction: Land, scan and establish a controlled position before contact.

commonErrors.error: Player holds the defender with the arms.
commonErrors.correction: Keep arms inside the body line and use feet and torso position.

commonErrors.error: Shepherd is too far from the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Move close enough to influence the defender while maintaining safe spacing.

commonErrors.error: Ruck continues blocking after the play has moved away.
commonErrors.correction: Release immediately and provide support.

commonErrors.error: Ruck watches only the defender.
commonErrors.correction: Continue scanning the ball and teammate throughout the action.

progressions: Allow controlled tackling.
Add a second defender.
Give the midfielder multiple disposal options.
Include a turnover exit in the opposite direction.
Begin with an opposed ruck contest.
regressions: Use a bump pad instead of a defender.
Walk through the landing and shepherd sequence.
successIndicators: Become involved again after the shepherd.
matchApplication: After a stoppage tap, the ruck is often in an ideal position to protect the first possession. A legal follow-up block can create time for a midfielder to handball, accelerate or connect with an outside runner before the ruck becomes a second disposal option.

title: Midfielder Read the Imperfect Tap
primarySkill: Stoppage reaction to imperfect taps
objective: Teach midfielders and rucks to remain connected when the tap misses its intended target and convert an imperfect contest into a useful possession or defensive response.
groundSize: A 16 × 16-metre stoppage area with four exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ruck and three midfielders around a central contest.
Add two shadow defenders.
Create four possible landing zones around the ruck point.
The feeder privately selects the actual landing zone.
The attacking group agrees on an intended hit zone.
The feeder may toss accurately or deliberately create a safe imperfect tap situation.
Mark four exit gates around the area.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking group communicates an intended hit zone.
The feeder tosses the football to the ruck.
The ruck attempts the planned tap but may receive a delivery that makes exact execution difficult.
All midfielders read the actual ball movement rather than continuing blindly to the planned position.
The nearest player attacks the football.
The other midfielders provide support, protect space or defend the turnover side.
The ruck follows the tap and contributes at ground level.
The team in possession exits through the nearest appropriate gate.
Shadow defenders attempt to intercept or force a fumble without tackling.
Rotate roles after four repetitions.
Award one point for the first clean possession and one point for a successful exit.
coachingPoints: Use the planned hit as a starting reference, not an unchangeable instruction.
Watch the ruck’s hand and the football’s initial movement.
The closest player attacks the ball decisively.
Other midfielders must adjust their support roles immediately.
Communicate changes using short calls.
Protect the dangerous opposition side when possession is uncertain.
The ruck must follow the ball rather than admire the tap.
Avoid having every midfielder collapse onto the same loose ball.
Select the exit based on where possession is won.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether midfielders continue running to an unavailable planned zone.
Speed of recognition after the tap changes direction.
Support spacing around the first possession.
Defensive positioning while the ball is loose.
Exit selection after possession is secured.

commonErrors.error: Midfielder ignores the actual ball and runs to the planned zone.
commonErrors.correction: Read the football immediately after contact and adjust the movement line.

commonErrors.error: All players collapse onto the loose ball.
commonErrors.correction: Send the nearest player while teammates hold support and defensive spacing.

commonErrors.error: Players stop communicating after a poor tap.
commonErrors.correction: Use immediate calls to identify ball, support and defensive roles.

commonErrors.error: Ruck remains at the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Follow the ball and become an extra ground-level number.

commonErrors.error: Team forces the original exit side.
commonErrors.correction: Use the gate that matches the location and direction of possession.

progressions: Increase defenders to controlled pressure.
Add an opposing ruck.
Remove visible landing zones.
Add a time limit for clearance.
Begin from boundary and centre-bounce positions.
Permit the defenders to counterattack after a turnover.
regressions: Use only two possible landing zones.
Roll the football into the imperfect zone.
Predetermine the first player to attack the ball.
successIndicators: Include the ruck in the follow-up phase.
Exit according to the position of the football.
matchApplication: Even well-planned stoppages rarely unfold perfectly. The ability to read an imperfect tap prevents players from running away from the football, improves ground-level coverage and helps the team retain structure during unpredictable contests.

title: Ruck Fundamentals Assessment Circuit
primarySkill: Ruck fundamentals assessment
objective: Assess whether players can combine the foundational ruck and stoppage skills introduced in RK-001 to RK-019 with safe, repeatable and tactically useful execution.
groundSize: Four assessment stations across approximately one-quarter of the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create four assessment stations.
Station 1: stance, approach and leap timing.
Station 2: preferred-hand and non-preferred-hand hit-zone accuracy.
Station 3: controlled opposed body position and defensive neutralisation.
Station 4: ruck-to-midfielder connection, follow-up and clearance.
Divide players evenly across stations.
Assign one coach or observer to each station where possible.
Use consistent scoring criteria for all players.
Allow appropriate contact and jump modifications for age, injury history and masters players.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete each station for five to seven minutes.
At Station 1, each player performs four variable approaches and is assessed on balance, adjustment, take-off timing and landing.
At Station 2, each player attempts eight taps to different zones, including at least two with the non-preferred hand.
At Station 3, players complete four controlled opposed contests, including one attacking and one neutralising task from each side.
At Station 4, groups complete six stoppage sequences requiring communication, a moving receiver, a support disposal and ruck follow-up.
Coaches record each skill as developing, competent or advanced.
Players rotate clockwise after the coach’s signal.
At the conclusion, each player receives one technical priority and one tactical priority for future training.
Repeat the circuit later in the program to measure improvement.
coachingPoints: Assess repeatability rather than rewarding one exceptional attempt.
Prioritise safe technique and legal body contact.
Observe both preferred and non-preferred sides.
Evaluate the quality and controllability of taps, not only first contact.
Include landing and follow-up behaviours in every assessment.
Assess communication before and during the contest.
Consider decision quality when the ball flight or tap is imperfect.
Modify jump and contact loads without removing the core assessment purpose.
Give feedback that is specific and actionable.
Record outcomes consistently for future comparison.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Consistency of starting stance and approach.
Timing of the leap and hand extension.
Accuracy, weight and direction of taps.
Ability to neutralise a lost contest.
Capacity to maintain technique across all stations.

commonErrors.error: Player treats each station as a maximum-intensity competition.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise repeatable technique, accuracy and safety over force.

commonErrors.error: Assessment focuses only on who touches the ball first.
commonErrors.correction: Score direction, control, landing and follow-up as well as first contact.

commonErrors.error: Player avoids the non-preferred hand.
commonErrors.correction: Require a minimum number of assessed non-preferred-hand attempts.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes unsafe jumping or body contact.
commonErrors.correction: Increase recovery or reduce repetitions while preserving assessment quality.

commonErrors.error: Feedback is too general.
commonErrors.correction: Give one observable technical action and one tactical action to improve.

commonErrors.error: Different coaches apply inconsistent standards.
commonErrors.correction: Use shared scoring definitions and review examples before beginning.

progressions: Repeat the circuit under greater opposition pressure.
Remove visible target zones.
Add boundary throw-in and centre-bounce stations.
Introduce scoreboard or time-pressure scenarios.
Compare individual results across multiple testing dates.
Add video review for advanced players.
regressions: Reduce jump height and repetition count.
Allow younger players to use soft footballs.
Replace competitive scoring with individual technique ratings.
successIndicators: Establish a balanced and repeatable stance.
Contact the football safely with an open hand.
Adjust when the planned outcome is unavailable.
Identify clear priorities for further development.
matchApplication: The circuit tests whether isolated ruck skills can be combined into functional stoppage performance. It provides coaches with evidence for selecting roles, planning individual development and deciding whether players are ready to progress into faster, more opposed and tactically complex ruck work.
relatedDrills: RK-001 – Balanced Ruck Stance and Ready Position
RK-019 – Midfielder Read the Imperfect Tap

title: Moving Drop-Zone Approach
primarySkill: Approaching a moving ruck contest
objective: Develop the ability to alter the approach line and arrive balanced when the expected ruck contest shifts into a different drop zone.
groundSize: A 15 × 12-metre area containing three separate contest zones.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark three two-metre-diameter drop zones across the working area.
Position the zones approximately three metres apart.
Place two target gates beyond the contest area.
One feeder stands five metres in front of the zones.
The ruck begins six metres away from the middle zone.
One retriever stands outside the working area.
Assign each drop zone a different colour.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ruck begins moving towards the middle contest zone.
As the player takes the first two steps, the feeder calls a colour.
The feeder tosses the football towards the corresponding drop zone.
The ruck adjusts the approach line using controlled, shortening steps.
The player jumps or remains grounded according to the ball flight.
The ruck directs the football through the nearest target gate.
The player lands, follows the tap and exits through the same gate.
Complete six repetitions before changing roles.
Award one point for arriving balanced and one point for directing the ball through the correct gate.
coachingPoints: Begin with enough control to change direction.
Read both the verbal cue and the football’s release.
Adjust progressively rather than cutting sharply at the final step.
Keep the chest and eyes directed towards the football.
Shorten the final steps when entering the new drop zone.
Select the safest available tapping hand.
Avoid jumping if the adjusted position does not permit a balanced take-off.
Follow the football immediately after contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The player’s speed before the zone is called.
How early the approach line begins to change.
The decision to jump or remain grounded.
Hand selection relative to the changed ball position.

commonErrors.error: Player runs too quickly to adjust.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the initial speed and accelerate only after the drop zone is identified.

commonErrors.error: Player changes direction with one large step.
commonErrors.correction: Use several short adjustment steps.

commonErrors.error: Player watches the coloured zone instead of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the colour, then return vision immediately to the ball.

commonErrors.error: Player jumps from an unstable position.
commonErrors.correction: Remain grounded or take an additional adjustment step.

commonErrors.error: Follow-up movement continues towards the original zone.
commonErrors.correction: Follow the actual direction of the tap.

progressions: Delay the colour call until later in the approach.
Remove the coloured ground markers.
Add a moving midfielder beyond each gate.
Add a passive opposing ruck.
