Allow the feeder to use deliberately imperfect tosses.
regressions: Call the zone before the ruck begins moving.
successIndicators: Arrive in the correct drop zone.
Select an appropriate take-off and tapping method.
matchApplication: Ruck contests frequently shift because of inconsistent throw-ups, boundary deliveries or congestion around the stoppage. A ruck who can redirect the approach without losing balance remains competitive when the ball does not enter the expected space.
relatedDrills: RK-019 – Midfielder Read the Imperfect Tap

title: Lateral Ruck Repositioning
primarySkill: Lateral repositioning before a ruck contest
objective: Teach players to move laterally around a stoppage while retaining balance, visual contact with the football and access to the preferred contest line.
groundSize: One 8 × 8-metre contest area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Place four positional markers around it at two-metre intervals.
One ruck begins at the front marker.
A feeder stands four metres away with a football.
A second player acts as a passive opponent occupying one side of the contest.
The passive opponent does not hold, push or jump.
Rotate all roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder identifies one of the four positional markers.
The ruck moves laterally around the contest point to reach that marker.
The player uses shuffle steps, pivots or short crossover recovery steps while keeping vision on the football.
The passive opponent occupies space and forces the ruck to choose a safe path.
Once the ruck arrives balanced, the feeder tosses the football.
The ruck performs a standing or low-jump palm towards a nominated target.
The player follows the tap for three metres.
Complete eight repetitions before rotating.
Award one point for balanced repositioning and one point for clean contact.
coachingPoints: Move the feet before using the upper body to protect space.
Keep the base wide enough to absorb incidental contact.
Avoid turning completely away from the football.
Use short steps when close to the contest point.
Do not cross the feet when under immediate pressure.
Re-establish a stable stance before jumping.
Position the hips and shoulders to preserve access to the ball.
Maintain legal separation from the opponent.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player remains balanced during lateral movement.
The amount of time visual contact with the football is lost.
Whether the player establishes the stance before the toss.
Use of legal body position near the passive opponent.

commonErrors.error: Player turns their back to the football.
commonErrors.correction: Use a side-on shuffle and keep the head and chest partly open.

commonErrors.error: Feet cross under pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the movement and use controlled shuffle steps.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches around the opponent instead of moving.
commonErrors.correction: Reposition the feet to create a clear line to the ball.

commonErrors.error: Player jumps before becoming balanced.
commonErrors.correction: Establish the stance and then compete.

commonErrors.error: Player uses extended arms to create space.
commonErrors.correction: Keep arms within the body line and use hip and shoulder position.

progressions: Increase passive pressure to controlled body contact.
Allow the opponent to reposition.
Add a late change of target marker.
Add a moving midfielder.
Progress to a live opposed tap contest.
regressions: Hold the football stationary for the final palm.
matchApplication: At congested stoppages, rucks often need to move around players or change sides before the ball is released. Efficient lateral movement helps the ruck protect the preferred approach, remain connected to midfield plans and avoid becoming trapped behind an opponent.
relatedDrills: RK-001 – Balanced Ruck Stance and Ready Position

title: Tap to Moving Midfielder
primarySkill: Tapping to a moving receiver
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to place the football into the path of a midfielder moving at speed rather than tapping towards a stationary position.
groundSize: A 12 × 12-metre area containing four running lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Create four curved running lanes entering the contest from different angles.
One ruck begins at the central point.
One midfielder begins five metres away.
One feeder stands beside the contest.
One retriever or support player waits beyond the exit gate.
Assign each running lane a colour.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder calls a lane colour.
The midfielder begins moving through the corresponding lane.
The feeder tosses the football as the midfielder approaches.
The ruck tracks both the football and the receiver’s movement.
The ruck directs the tap one to two metres ahead of the midfielder.
The midfielder collects without stopping and exits through the gate.
The ruck follows to provide a support option.
Complete six repetitions before rotating roles.
Award one point for a collectable tap and one point when the midfielder maintains running speed.
coachingPoints: Tap to where the midfielder will arrive, not where the player begins.
Match the tap weight to the receiver’s speed.
Keep communication short and consistent.
Avoid staring at the receiver after the ball is tossed.
Use the contact angle that leads the player into space.
The midfielder should hold the starting position until the cue.
The ruck must follow the clearance line after landing.
Reset spacing before each repetition.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The timing of the midfielder’s movement.
Whether the tap leads or trails the receiver.
The relationship between tap weight and running speed.
The ruck’s visual scanning before the toss.
Whether the midfielder collects without stopping.

commonErrors.error: Tap is delivered to the receiver’s starting position.
commonErrors.correction: Aim into the space ahead of the moving player.

commonErrors.error: Tap travels too far for the receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce force and shorten the target distance.

commonErrors.error: Midfielder moves before the cue.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the starting position until the lane is called.

commonErrors.error: Ruck watches the runner and misses the football.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the runner early, then track the ball through contact.

commonErrors.error: Receiver slows before collecting.
commonErrors.correction: Improve the lead distance and tap weight.

progressions: Call the lane after the football is released.
Add a passive defending midfielder.
Allow the receiver to choose the lane.
Add an opposing ruck.
Require a second disposal after collection.
regressions: Use a stationary palm without jumping.
successIndicators: Deliver the football into running space.
Match tap weight to player speed.
Allow the receiver to collect without stopping.
Follow the clearance as a support option.
matchApplication: Successful stoppage connection depends on the ruck delivering into moving space. Leading a midfielder allows the receiver to accelerate away from congestion and reduces the chance of immediate tackling pressure.
relatedDrills: RK-015 – Tap Weight and Distance Control
RK-019 – Midfielder Read the Imperfect Tap

title: Landing Escape and Re-Entry
primarySkill: Moving safely out of and back into a stoppage
objective: Teach the ruck to land safely, escape the immediate congestion and re-enter the play through a useful support or pressure lane.
groundSize: A 14 × 14-metre contest area with four re-entry gates.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central ruck contest.
Place four two-metre-wide re-entry gates around the area.
One ruck, one midfielder, one feeder and two passive traffic players participate.
The traffic players stand near the landing area and move at walking pace.
The ruck must not push through the traffic players.
One exit gate is positioned beyond the contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder tosses the football to the ruck.
The ruck palms the ball towards the midfielder.
The ruck lands and identifies the clearest re-entry gate.
The player exits the immediate contest area through that gate.
The ruck then curves back into the play as either a receiver, shepherd or pressure player.
The midfielder carries or handballs towards the exit gate.
The traffic players create moving obstacles without applying contact.
Complete five repetitions before rotating roles.
Award one point for a safe escape and one point for useful re-entry involvement.
coachingPoints: Stabilise the landing before changing direction.
Scan immediately for players around the feet and landing path.
Move away from the densest congestion rather than forcing through it.
Use a curved re-entry line that keeps the player connected to the football.
Communicate whether providing support, protection or pressure.
Avoid running directly behind the ball carrier.
Re-enter at controlled speed.
Transition defensively if possession changes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Awareness of players around the contest.
Selection of the safest escape route.
Whether the ruck becomes disconnected from the play.
Quality and timing of the re-entry line.

commonErrors.error: Ruck pushes through congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Use the clearest outside route and re-enter from space.

commonErrors.error: Player changes direction before landing securely.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the landing before accelerating.

commonErrors.error: Ruck runs away from the play entirely.
commonErrors.correction: Curve back towards the next likely possession.

commonErrors.error: Re-entry line follows directly behind the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Provide an inside, outside or trailing angle.

commonErrors.error: Player re-enters too quickly and causes contact.
commonErrors.correction: Control the speed and scan before crossing another player’s line.

progressions: Allow traffic players to apply shadow pressure.
Add a live defender.
Remove coloured re-entry gates.
Add a turnover transition.
Require the ruck to receive a handball after re-entry.
successIndicators: Remain involved in attack or defence.
matchApplication: Rucks frequently land inside the most congested part of a stoppage. Moving safely out of that space and re-entering from a better angle allows the player to support the clearance, protect a teammate or apply pressure without creating further congestion.
relatedDrills: RK-019 – Midfielder Read the Imperfect Tap

title: Second-Effort Handball Link
primarySkill: Ruck involvement in the second disposal
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to follow the tap, receive a return handball and connect the clearance to an outside player.
groundSize: A 20 × 15-metre area with inside and outside support lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central stoppage point.
Create an inside support lane and an outside release lane.
One ruck, one inside midfielder and one outside midfielder form the attacking group.
One feeder controls the toss.
One shadow defender pressures the inside midfielder.
The ruck must follow into a different lane from the first receiver.
howTheDrillWorks:
The group communicates the intended hit zone.
The feeder tosses the football.
The ruck taps to the inside midfielder.
The ruck lands and accelerates into the support lane.
The inside midfielder collects under shadow pressure.
The midfielder handballs back to the moving ruck.
The ruck receives and immediately handballs to the outside midfielder.
The outside midfielder exits through either gate.
If the first possession is fumbled, all players react to the loose ball.
Rotate roles after three repetitions.
Award one point for each completed connection and one point for the exit.
coachingPoints: The ruck must move immediately after landing.
Present in a different lane from the first receiver.
Show the hands early and communicate.
Receive the return handball while moving.
Turn the shoulders towards the outside option before possession arrives.
Release the handball quickly without stopping.
Keep the outside midfielder wide until the ball is secured.
React to imperfect taps or disposals rather than ending the repetition.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The speed of the ruck’s second effort.
Whether the support lane is clear.
Timing and quality of the return handball.
The ruck’s body orientation before receiving.
Whether the outside player maintains width.
Decision making after a fumble or poor tap.

commonErrors.error: Ruck remains at the original contest.
commonErrors.correction: Move immediately into the marked support lane.

commonErrors.error: Ruck follows the first midfielder’s line.
commonErrors.correction: Use a separate inside or outside angle.

commonErrors.error: Player stops to receive the handball.
commonErrors.correction: Time the run so possession is received in motion.

commonErrors.error: Ruck turns after receiving.
commonErrors.correction: Open the shoulders towards the next option before the ball arrives.

commonErrors.error: Outside midfielder moves into congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the second disposal is completed.

progressions: Add a defender against the ruck.
Allow the inside midfielder to bypass the ruck when appropriate.
Remove marked support lanes.
Add a kicking finish.
Include a turnover counterattack.
regressions: Begin with the ruck already on the ground.
successIndicators: Present in a clear support lane.
Connect cleanly with the outside player.
Adapt when the planned sequence breaks down.
matchApplication: A ruck can create a numerical advantage by becoming the second link in a stoppage clearance. Receiving the return handball helps the team move the football from congestion to an outside runner before the opposition can reset.

title: Mobile Boundary Throw-In Connection
primarySkill: Moving boundary-stoppage connection
objective: Develop coordinated movement between the ruck and midfielders at a boundary throw-in, including approach adjustment, moving hit zones and clearance back into the field.
groundSize: A 20 × 15-metre area positioned beside a marked boundary line.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a 20-metre boundary line.
Position a feeder outside the boundary.
Mark three hit zones: front, rear and corridor-side.
One ruck and three midfielders form the attacking group.
Add one shadow defender.
Create a corridor exit gate 10 metres inside the field.
Midfielders begin from balanced inside, outside and defensive positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking group communicates a preferred hit zone.
The feeder delivers a boundary throw-in with controlled variation.
The ruck uses a curved approach and adjusts to the ball flight.
The nominated midfielder moves late into the planned zone.
The ruck directs the football into the receiver’s path.
The other midfielders provide support and defensive coverage.
The shadow defender pressures the first possession.
The team attempts to clear through the corridor exit.
The ruck lands and follows the clearance.
If the ball travels towards the boundary, players must keep it in play before exiting.
Rotate roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Keep the ruck’s body open towards the field.
Avoid tapping blindly towards the boundary.
Use a curved approach that allows late adjustment.
The receiver should move after the throw has established its flight.
Maintain one defensive-side midfielder.
Use the corridor-side support player when the initial receiver is pressured.
The ruck must follow inside rather than drifting over the line.
React immediately if the football falls short or deep.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The ruck’s approach line and body orientation.
Whether the football is directed away from the boundary.
Clearance direction after possession is won.

commonErrors.error: Ruck faces completely towards the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Open the chest towards the field and corridor-side zones.

commonErrors.error: Midfielder fills the hit zone too early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the starting position until the throw is in flight.

commonErrors.error: Tap repeatedly travels over the line.
commonErrors.correction: Contact the outer panel and finish back into the field.

commonErrors.error: All midfielders attack the first possession.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain support width and defensive-side coverage.

commonErrors.error: Ruck follows outside the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Land and move inside towards the clearance.

progressions: Add an opposing ruck.
Increase midfield pressure.
Allow the ruck to change the hit zone after reading the throw.
Remove visible hit-zone gates.
Add a kick to a leading target after clearance.
successIndicators: Adjust to the boundary throw-in flight.
Include the ruck in the follow-up.
matchApplication: Boundary stoppages restrict space and increase the risk of the football leaving play again. Coordinated ruck and midfield movement helps a team keep the ball inside the boundary, win the first possession and escape towards the corridor.
relatedDrills: RK-019 – Midfielder Read the Imperfect Tap

title: Centre Bounce Exit-Lane Selection
primarySkill: Selecting a clearance lane after the centre bounce
objective: Teach the ruck and midfield group to connect the centre-bounce tap with the most appropriate available exit lane rather than forcing a predetermined direction.
groundSize: A centre-square-sized area with four clearance gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck contest and four exit gates.
One ruck and three midfielders form the attacking group.
Add two shadow defenders.
One feeder delivers a centre-bounce-style toss.
Before each repetition, the coach secretly closes one exit gate by placing a defender or marker in it.
Players must identify the available space during the contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ruck and midfielders organise their starting positions.
The feeder prepares the toss while the coach closes one gate.
The feeder releases the football.
The ruck competes and directs the tap towards a moving midfielder.
The receiver collects and scans the exit options.
Support players adjust their movement towards the open gates.
The team exits through an available lane using up to two disposals.
The ruck follows as a support player.
Shadow defenders attempt to influence the receiver without tackling.
Rotate roles every four repetitions.
Award one point for the first possession and one point for selecting an open exit.
coachingPoints: Scan exit lanes before and during the contest.
Do not commit every player to the planned side.
The receiver must recognise pressure immediately.
Support players should spread into different lanes.
The ruck should follow the most likely clearance route.
Use the hit zone to create access, not to dictate the entire play.
Avoid carrying the football towards a closed gate.
Maintain defensive coverage if possession is lost.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players identify the closed gate.
Whether the group forces the original plan.

commonErrors.error: Receiver runs towards the planned gate without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Lift the eyes immediately after possession and identify pressure.

commonErrors.error: All support players move into one lane.
commonErrors.correction: Assign inside, outside and trailing options.

commonErrors.error: Ruck follows the wrong side of the clearance.
commonErrors.correction: Track the first possession and move towards the likely release.

commonErrors.error: Team stops when the preferred gate is closed.
commonErrors.correction: Use the nearest open lane and continue the sequence.

commonErrors.error: Players ignore turnover positioning.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one midfielder balanced on the defensive side.

progressions: Close two exit gates.
Add live controlled defenders.
Allow the ruck to choose the hit zone.
Remove coloured gates and use field landmarks.
Finish with a kick inside 50.
regressions: Close the gate before players take their positions.
successIndicators: Connect the tap with a moving receiver.
Include the ruck in the clearance.
matchApplication: Centre clearances rarely unfold exactly as planned. Selecting the open lane after possession allows the team to avoid pressure, exploit space and move the football forward without forcing a congested or blocked exit.

title: Ruck–Rover Role Rotation
primarySkill: Rotating ruck and ground-level roles
objective: Develop understanding between rucks and midfielders by requiring players to rotate between the aerial contest, first possession and support roles.
groundSize: A 15 × 15-metre area with three exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Players work in groups of three.
Assign the roles of ruck, rover and support midfielder.
Mark one central contest and three exit gates.
One feeder controls the football.
Add one shadow defender if numbers allow.
Players rotate roles after every repetition rather than after a full set.
howTheDrillWorks:
The group quickly identifies the three roles.
The feeder tosses the football.
The ruck directs the tap towards the rover.
The rover collects or contests the ground ball.
The support midfielder presents through an open lane.
The ruck follows and becomes a secondary option.
The group completes up to two disposals and exits through a gate.
Immediately after the repetition, the ruck becomes the rover, the rover becomes support and support becomes the ruck.
The next repetition begins after a short reset.
Award one point for correct role execution and one point for a successful exit.
coachingPoints: Identify the responsibilities of each role before the toss.
Rucks should experience the timing required by the rover.
Midfielders should experience the difficulty of directing a tap.
The rover attacks the ball while support holds space.
The ruck follows after landing.
Communicate the rotation clearly.
Maintain technique despite frequent role changes.
Adjust jump requirements for players who are not regular rucks.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether technique deteriorates as roles change.

commonErrors.error: Players forget the new role.
commonErrors.correction: Call the rotation aloud before resetting.

commonErrors.error: Support player attacks the same ball as the rover.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width and wait for the release.

commonErrors.error: Non-specialist ruck uses unsafe jumping technique.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce jump height and focus on controlled standing palms.

commonErrors.error: Ruck does not follow the tap.
commonErrors.correction: Make follow-up movement a required scoring condition.

commonErrors.error: Players rush the reset.
commonErrors.correction: Establish positions and communication before the next toss.

progressions: Add controlled opposition.
Remove role markers.
Use different hit zones.
Add turnover exits.
Require players to nominate the best role execution after each set.
regressions: Keep players in each role for three repetitions.
successIndicators: Execute the responsibilities of each position.
Follow the tap and support the clearance.
Demonstrate improved understanding of teammates’ movements.
matchApplication: Understanding multiple stoppage roles improves coordination and communication. Rucks gain insight into the timing midfielders require, while midfielders better understand the ruck’s visual and technical demands.
relatedDrills: RK-019 – Midfielder Read the Imperfect Tap

title: Repeat Stoppage Relocation
primarySkill: Moving between consecutive stoppages
objective: Develop the ability of the ruck and midfield group to move quickly from one stoppage location to another, reorganise roles and execute the next contest without losing structure.
groundSize: A 35 × 25-metre area containing four stoppage points.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark four stoppage points across the area.
Each point should represent a different field location.
One attacking group contains a ruck and three midfielders.
Add two shadow defenders.
The coach or feeder stands centrally with several footballs.
Mark one exit gate near each stoppage point.
Predetermine a safe running route between locations.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach calls the number of the first stoppage point.
Players move into balanced starting positions.
The feeder tosses the football and the group completes a ruck-to-clearance sequence.
Once the ball exits, the coach immediately calls the next stoppage number.
All players relocate and reorganise while the feeder prepares another football.
Roles may remain the same or be changed by the coach.
Complete three consecutive stoppages before a recovery period.
Run four sets, changing the order of locations.
Award one point for correct organisation and one point for each successful clearance.
If the defenders win possession, they exit through the nearest gate before all players relocate.
coachingPoints: Move quickly but arrive under control.
Communicate roles while travelling between stoppages.
The ruck should identify the new ball-delivery type and approach space.
Midfielders must establish balanced spacing rather than simply following the ball.
Preserve one defensive-side position.
Reset the hit-zone call before each contest.
Maintain skill execution as fatigue rises.
Transition immediately when possession changes.
Protect older or returning players with appropriate running and jump loads.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players crowd the new contest.
Ruck approach adjustment at different locations.
Players who repeatedly arrive late or lose role clarity.

commonErrors.error: Players sprint to the ball and arrive disorganised.
commonErrors.correction: Move quickly, then slow early enough to establish positions.

commonErrors.error: Communication begins only after arrival.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm roles and hit-zone ideas while travelling.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders follow identical running lines.
commonErrors.correction: Spread into inside, outside and defensive positions.

commonErrors.error: Ruck uses the same approach at every location.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust to the boundary, centre or congested setup.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes poor technique.
commonErrors.correction: Increase recovery or reduce repetitions before quality deteriorates.

progressions: Add live controlled opposition.
Shorten the organisation time.
Include a fifth stoppage location.
Vary between throw-up and boundary-style delivery.
Add scoreboard consequences for each set.
matchApplication: Matches contain repeated stoppages across changing areas of the ground. Rucks and midfielders must recover, relocate and reorganise quickly without losing role clarity or allowing fatigue to reduce technique and decision quality.
relatedDrills: RK-019 – Midfielder Read the Imperfect Tap

title: Ruck Movement and Connection Assessment
primarySkill: Assessment of moving ruck and stoppage connection
objective: Assess whether players can maintain safe ruck technique, coordinated midfield movement and useful follow-up involvement while the contest location, receiver and clearance direction change.
groundSize: Approximately one-third of the ground containing three assessment stations.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create three assessment stations.
Station 1: moving drop-zone approach and lateral repositioning.
Station 2: tap to a moving receiver and second-effort handball connection.
Station 3: consecutive stoppage relocation and exit-lane selection.
Divide players evenly between stations.
Assign an observer to each station where possible.
Use developing, competent and advanced ratings.
Modify jump volume and running distance where required.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete six to eight minutes at each station.
At Station 1, the ruck responds to changing drop zones and performs six adjusted contests.
At Station 2, the ruck connects with three different receiver movements and follows into the second disposal.
At Station 3, the group completes three consecutive stoppages at different locations.
Coaches assess movement control, communication, tap quality, receiver timing and follow-up involvement.
Players rotate after the coach’s signal.
Each player must perform at least one ruck role and one midfield role where physically appropriate.
Coaches record one movement strength and one priority for improvement.
Finish with one full-group repetition combining all three assessment themes.
Retain results for comparison later in the chapter.
coachingPoints: Assess movement quality rather than running speed alone.
Observe whether the ruck remains balanced while adjusting.
Evaluate taps according to the receiver’s movement.
Include landing, escape and re-entry in the assessment.
Check whether the ruck contributes to the second disposal.
Assess communication during relocation.
Observe structure when players are fatigued.
Reward adaptive decisions rather than rigid execution.
Apply consistent standards across all groups.
Reduce physical demand before technique becomes unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Tap weight relative to receiver speed.
Adaptation when the planned outcome changes.

commonErrors.error: Players prioritise speed over balance.
commonErrors.correction: Slow the approach enough to preserve controlled footwork and take-off.

commonErrors.error: Assessment records only the first tap.
commonErrors.correction: Include receiver connection, follow-up and clearance outcome.

commonErrors.error: Ruck becomes stationary after landing.
commonErrors.correction: Require second-phase involvement in every assessed repetition.

commonErrors.error: Players lose structure during repeat stoppages.
commonErrors.correction: Assess organisation and spacing before allowing the next toss.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue changes safe movement technique.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the work period or increase recovery.

commonErrors.error: Coaches use different rating standards.
commonErrors.correction: Review the developing, competent and advanced criteria before starting.

progressions: Repeat with controlled opposition.
Remove visible movement and exit markers.
Add boundary and centre-bounce variations.
Add time and scoreboard pressure.
Compare results with RK-020 assessment data.
Use video review for advanced players.
regressions: Assess each station in separate sessions.
Reduce the number of consecutive stoppages.
Use only two receiver movement patterns.
Reduce jump volume for masters or returning players.
successIndicators: Adjust approach lines without losing balance.
Reposition laterally while tracking the football.
Select useful escape and re-entry paths.
Maintain communication and spacing under fatigue.
Demonstrate clear progress from the fundamentals assessment.
matchApplication: The assessment establishes whether players can transfer basic ruck technique into moving stoppage situations. It identifies who can adjust to changing ball locations, connect with moving midfielders and remain involved through repeated phases of play.

title: Curved Approach Against Moving Opposition
primarySkill: Maintaining an effective approach line against a repositioning opponent
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to preserve a balanced approach and access the football when an opposing ruck changes position before the contest.
groundSize: One 12 × 10-metre contest area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central two-metre-diameter drop zone.
Create two curved approach lanes entering from opposite sides.
One working ruck begins five metres from the contest.
One passive opponent begins beside the drop zone.
The passive opponent may move around the edge of the zone but may not block with extended arms or initiate forceful contact.
A feeder stands four metres from the contest.
Place one target gate on each side of the area.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working ruck begins approaching the central drop zone.
Before the feeder releases the football, the passive opponent moves to occupy part of the preferred approach line.
The working ruck reads the opponent and adjusts onto a safe curved path.
The feeder tosses the football into the drop zone.
The ruck establishes a balanced take-off position without running through the opponent.
The player palms the football through the most accessible target gate.
Both players land or reset without continuing body contact.
Complete four repetitions before changing the active and passive roles.
Award one point for maintaining safe access and one point for a controlled directional tap.
coachingPoints: Scan the opponent before committing fully to the approach.
Change the approach gradually rather than cutting sharply.
Protect the approach line with foot position rather than extended arms.
Keep the eyes returning to the football after scanning the opponent.
Avoid becoming trapped directly behind the opposing ruck.
Shorten the final steps to restore balance.
Select the available hand and target rather than forcing the original plan.
Land away from the opponent’s feet where possible.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ruck notices the opponent’s movement early.
The control of the altered approach line.
Whether the player attempts to run through occupied space.
The amount of time visual contact with the football is lost.
Hand and target selection after the approach changes.

commonErrors.error: Player continues along a blocked approach line.
commonErrors.correction: Scan earlier and curve towards the open side of the contest.

commonErrors.error: Ruck makes a sharp final-step cut.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust progressively using several shorter steps.

commonErrors.error: Player pushes the opponent away with an arm.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the arm inside the body line and use foot position to preserve space.

commonErrors.error: Ruck loses sight of the football while watching the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Use a quick scan and return vision to the ball immediately.

commonErrors.error: Player forces the original target despite poor access.
commonErrors.correction: Select the safest available hand and hit zone.

progressions: Allow the opponent to apply controlled body pressure.
Delay the opponent’s movement until later in the approach.
Add a moving midfielder to each target gate.
Allow both rucks to compete for the tap.
Remove the marked approach lanes.
regressions: Announce the occupied side before the approach.
successIndicators: Recognise when the preferred line is unavailable.
Maintain visual contact with the football.
Produce a useful tap from the altered position.
matchApplication: Opposing rucks regularly change their starting position to interrupt an approach or protect a preferred space. A controlled curved adjustment allows the ruck to remain competitive without creating late collisions or sacrificing balance.

title: Aborted Leap and Grounded Re-Contest
primarySkill: Safely abandoning an unsuitable ruck leap
objective: Teach players to recognise when a planned leap is no longer safe or effective, remain grounded and compete through balance, positioning and follow-up effort.
groundSize: A 10 × 10-metre contest area.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central expected drop zone.
Position two ground-level target zones three metres away.
One ruck begins four metres from the contest.
One feeder stands to the side.
The feeder alternates between normal vertical tosses and deliberately low or short tosses.
One retriever waits outside the working area.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ruck begins a controlled approach expecting to jump.
The feeder delivers either a normal toss or a low, short toss.
The player reads the flight during the approach.
For a normal toss, the ruck completes the jump and palm.
For a low or short toss, the player abandons the leap, lowers the centre of gravity and competes from the ground.
The grounded player directs the football into the nearest target zone or secures the loose ball.
The player follows with a handball to the feeder.
Complete eight repetitions before rotating roles.
Award one point for the correct jump decision and one point for a controlled follow-up action.
coachingPoints: Decide according to the actual ball flight rather than the original intention.
Reduce speed immediately when the ball falls short.
Keep both feet available for adjustment.
Do not launch from an unstable or crowded position.
Use an open palm when the football remains reachable.
Lower the body safely for a ground-level contest.
Continue into the second effort after abandoning the leap.
Treat remaining grounded as a tactical decision, not a failed attempt.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How quickly the player identifies the unsuitable toss.
Whether approach speed is reduced safely.
The player’s balance when cancelling the jump.
Ground-level hand shape and body position.
Whether the player remains involved after the initial decision.
Any unnecessary jumping at low footballs.

commonErrors.error: Player jumps despite the football falling short.
commonErrors.correction: Cancel the leap early and move into a grounded contest position.

commonErrors.error: Player stops completely after abandoning the jump.
commonErrors.correction: Continue towards the ball under control and complete the second effort.

commonErrors.error: Player bends only at the waist.
commonErrors.correction: Lower through the ankles, knees and hips.

commonErrors.error: Grounded contact becomes a closed-fist punch.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the hand open and guide the football into a defensible area.

commonErrors.error: Player is disappointed and disengages.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that the correct decision is more important than completing the planned jump.

progressions: Add a passive opposing ruck.
Include an attacking and defensive target.
Add a midfielder reacting to the low ball.
Delay the change in ball flight.
Allow the feeder to create lateral variation as well as short deliveries.
regressions: Use only two predictable toss heights.
successIndicators: Identify when a leap is unsuitable.
Maintain balance while cancelling the take-off.
matchApplication: Unpredictable throw-ups, blocked approaches and low boundary deliveries can make a planned leap unsafe. A ruck who can abandon the jump and remain involved prevents the opposition from gaining an uncontested ground-level advantage.
relatedDrills: RK-031 – Curved Approach Against Moving Opposition

title: Ruck Follow-Up Tackle Pressure
primarySkill: Applying pressure after the ruck contest
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to recover from the aerial contest and apply immediate, controlled pressure when the opposition wins the first possession.
groundSize: A 15 × 12-metre area with two defensive exit gates.
equipment: Optional tackle bags for introductory repetitions
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Position one ruck, one opposition midfielder, one attacking midfielder and one feeder.
Add one support player beyond the contest.
The feeder may direct the tap or loose football towards either midfielder.
Mark two exit gates eight metres from the stoppage.
Begin with touch pressure before progressing to controlled tackling.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder tosses the football to the ruck.
The ruck attempts to direct the tap to the attacking midfielder.
On selected repetitions, the feeder or coach creates an opposition win.
The ruck lands, identifies the opposition ball carrier and closes space.
The player applies touch, wrap or controlled tackle pressure according to the drill phase.
The attacking midfielder protects the inside release or pressures the support option.
The opposition attempts to exit through either gate.
If the ruck forces a fumble or turnover, the attacking group counterattacks.
Rotate roles after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Complete the landing before changing direction.
Locate the football and ball carrier immediately.
Close space under control rather than charging past the player.
Approach from an angle that limits the inside exit.
Keep the head safely to one side during controlled tackling.
Use legal tackle height and technique.
Communicate pressure direction to teammates.
Continue applying pressure if the first tackle is avoided.
Transition into attack after a turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Time taken to identify the opposition possession.
Balance during the first defensive steps.
Legal contact height and head position.
Whether the ruck stops after one missed effort.

commonErrors.error: Ruck watches the tap and reacts late.
commonErrors.correction: Locate the next possession immediately after landing.

commonErrors.error: Player sprints directly at the ball carrier and is sidestepped.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and approach from an angle.

commonErrors.error: Tackle contact is too high.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the body and target the legal tackle zone.

commonErrors.error: Ruck pressures the same side as the teammate.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and close the opposite escape lane.

commonErrors.error: Player stops after the first missed tackle.
commonErrors.correction: Recover and continue tracking until the ball exits.

progressions: Increase to live controlled tackling.
Add a second opposition support player.
Begin with an opposed ruck contest.
Add a turnover scoring gate.
Introduce repeated contests with limited recovery.
regressions: Replace the ball carrier with a tackle bag.
successIndicators: Apply legal pressure or tackling technique.
matchApplication: A ruck cannot assume the team will win every tap. Immediate follow-up pressure can prevent an opposition clearance, force a rushed disposal or create a turnover before the ball escapes congestion.

title: Tap-and-Chase Space Recovery
primarySkill: Following a long tap into open space
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to deliver the football beyond immediate congestion and accelerate after the tap to support or recover the loose ball.
groundSize: A 20 × 12-metre area with three long hit zones.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Create three hit zones five to seven metres away.
Place a finishing gate another eight metres beyond the zones.
One ruck, one midfielder, one feeder and one retriever work in each group.
The midfielder begins beside the ruck and runs towards the called zone.
The ruck must follow the ball after tapping.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder calls one of the three hit zones.
The midfielder accelerates towards the zone.
The feeder tosses the football to the ruck.
The ruck delivers a weighted tap into the open space ahead of the midfielder.
The ruck lands and immediately chases the football.
The midfielder attempts to collect in stride.
If the midfielder fumbles, the ruck recovers the loose football.
The player in possession handballs to the other player before both run through the finishing gate.
Complete six repetitions before rotating.
Award one point for an accurate long tap and one point for successful recovery and connection.
coachingPoints: Use a stronger open-hand finish without punching.
Place the football into reachable open space.
Begin the chase immediately after landing.
Track the ball rather than only the midfielder.
Maintain separation between the ruck and receiver.
Communicate who will collect a loose football.
Keep the disposal clean while moving at speed.
Reduce tap distance when accuracy deteriorates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ball leads the midfielder appropriately.

commonErrors.error: Tap travels too far for either player.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce force and place the ball into recoverable space.

commonErrors.error: Ruck remains at the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Chase immediately as part of the scoring requirement.

commonErrors.error: Both players reach the loose ball from the same line.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and approach from separate angles.

commonErrors.error: Ruck watches the midfielder instead of the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Track the football’s bounce and movement.

commonErrors.error: Disposal quality deteriorates at speed.
commonErrors.correction: Control the final steps before handballing.

progressions: Add a trailing defender.
Change the finishing gate after collection.
Increase the number of hit zones.
Allow the midfielder to choose the running lane.
Begin with an opposed ruck contest.
successIndicators: Complete a clean disposal at speed.
matchApplication: A longer tap can bypass congestion and create a race into open space. The ruck’s follow-up run ensures the team retains an extra number if the receiver fumbles or requires immediate support.
relatedDrills: RK-015 – Tap Weight and Distance Control

title: Midfield Rotation Around the Ruck
primarySkill: Coordinating midfield movement around a stationary ruck reference
objective: Teach midfielders to rotate through inside, outside and defensive positions without crowding the ruck or losing balanced stoppage coverage.
groundSize: A 15 × 15-metre stoppage area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Position three midfield role markers around the contest: inside, outside and defensive.
One ruck begins centrally.
Three midfielders occupy the role markers.
One feeder holds the football.
The coach identifies a rotation direction before each repetition.
Place an exit gate beyond each midfield position.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin in the three midfield roles.
The coach calls “left”, “right” or “hold”.
On a left or right call, the midfielders rotate one role around the ruck.
Players communicate the new role while maintaining spacing.
The feeder tosses the football once the rotation is complete.
The ruck selects a hit zone based on the final structure.
The nominated receiver attacks the tap.
The remaining midfielders provide support and defensive coverage.
The group exits through an appropriate gate.
Rotate the ruck and midfield roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Rotate around the contest rather than through the ruck’s space.
Communicate role changes during movement.
Arrive in a balanced stance before the toss.
Preserve one defensive-side player.
Do not allow two midfielders to occupy the same line.
The ruck must recognise the completed structure before selecting the hit.
Support players should move after the receiver commits.
Maintain flexibility rather than treating the markers as fixed match positions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players rotate without crossing the ruck’s area.
The ruck’s recognition of the final formation.
Support and defensive movement after the tap.
Whether players become dependent on ground markers.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders cut through the ruck contest.
commonErrors.correction: Rotate around the perimeter and protect the approach space.

commonErrors.error: Two players arrive at the same marker.
commonErrors.correction: Call roles clearly during the rotation.

commonErrors.error: Defensive balance disappears.
commonErrors.correction: Ensure one player finishes on the defensive side.

commonErrors.error: Players rotate but remain upright and inactive.
commonErrors.correction: Arrive in a balanced stance ready to accelerate.

commonErrors.error: Ruck taps before the structure is set.
commonErrors.correction: Scan and confirm the final positions before the feeder releases.

progressions: Remove the role markers.
Add passive opposition midfielders.
Call the rotation later.
Allow one midfielder to fake a rotation.
Add a turnover transition.
regressions: Pause before the toss to confirm each position.
successIndicators: Connect the final structure with an appropriate hit zone.
matchApplication: Midfielders frequently rotate before a stoppage to create match-ups, disguise intended movements or respond to opposition positioning. Coordinated rotation preserves the ruck’s space and keeps the group balanced if the tap is lost.

title: Boundary Throw-In Front-or-Back Read
primarySkill: Reading front and rear hit opportunities at a boundary throw-in
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to read whether the front or rear hit zone is available and connect with the appropriate midfielder at a boundary throw-in.
groundSize: A 16 × 14-metre area beside a marked boundary line.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a boundary line and central throw-in point.
Place one front hit-zone gate and one rear hit-zone gate.
Position one midfielder near each zone.
One ruck begins three metres inside the boundary.
One feeder stands outside the line.
Add one passive defender who may occupy either hit zone.
Create a corridor exit gate 10 metres inside the field.
howTheDrillWorks:
The passive defender selects either the front or rear hit zone to occupy.
The ruck and midfielders scan the defensive position.
The feeder delivers the boundary throw-in.
The ruck adjusts the approach while keeping the chest open towards the field.
The player directs the tap to the unoccupied hit zone.
The corresponding midfielder moves late to receive.
The other midfielder provides support or protects the defensive side.
The group clears through the corridor gate.
The ruck follows the play inside the field.
Rotate roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Identify the defender’s position before the football reaches its peak.
Keep both front and rear options available through body orientation.
Avoid leaning towards the preferred hit zone too early.
Use appropriate touch for a short rear tap.
Direct front taps into the receiver’s path.
Keep the football inside the boundary.
The non-receiving midfielder must remain connected.
Follow the clearance into the field.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ruck scans the defender.
Accuracy to front and rear targets.
Whether the ruck reveals the tap early.
Direction of the clearance after possession.

commonErrors.error: Ruck taps to the occupied zone.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the defender and choose the available side.

commonErrors.error: Player turns the body too early.
commonErrors.correction: Stay open and disguise the intended contact.

commonErrors.error: Rear tap travels too far or high.
commonErrors.correction: Use softer wrist control and a shorter finish.

commonErrors.error: Front midfielder moves before the throw.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the starting position and accelerate late.

commonErrors.error: Non-receiving midfielder becomes inactive.
commonErrors.correction: Provide support or defensive-side coverage.

progressions: Allow the defender to change zones during the throw.
Add an opposing ruck.
Remove the visible hit-zone gates.
Increase midfield pressure.
Add a turnover clearance along the boundary.
regressions: Announce the occupied zone before setup.
Practise only front or rear taps for one set.
successIndicators: Maintain access to front and rear options.
Support the clearance inside the field.
matchApplication: Boundary stoppages often provide only narrow front and rear hit zones. Reading which space is available prevents predictable taps and allows the midfield group to escape repeated congestion near the line.
relatedDrills: RK-015 – Tap Weight and Distance Control
RK-031 – Curved Approach Against Moving Opposition
RK-035 – Midfield Rotation Around the Ruck

title: Centre-Bounce Safe Landing Corridor
primarySkill: Protecting a safe landing corridor at the centre bounce
objective: Teach rucks and midfielders to preserve clear take-off and landing corridors while still creating effective centre-bounce hit and clearance options.
groundSize: A centre-square-sized area with two marked landing corridors.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark two opposing ruck approach and landing corridors.
Position one ruck at each end.
Add three midfielders for the attacking side.
One feeder delivers a centre-bounce-style toss.
Midfielders may not enter either landing corridor before both rucks have landed.
Place four clearance gates outside the contest.
Begin with the second ruck passive before progressing.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both rucks begin in their approach lanes.
Midfielders organise around the outside of the marked corridors.
The feeder tosses the football.
The rucks approach and compete at controlled intensity.
Midfielders move towards the intended hit zones without entering the landing paths.
Once both rucks have landed, players may close into the contest.
The team in possession clears through an available gate.
Both rucks follow the play after safely exiting their landing area.
Rotate rucks and midfielders after four repetitions.
Stop immediately if a player enters an unsafe landing space.
coachingPoints: Preserve a direct and uncluttered ruck approach.
Midfielders should begin outside the landing corridors.
Move towards hit zones from angles that do not cross underneath the rucks.
Rucks must avoid drifting excessively across the contest.
Land with awareness of the opposing ruck.
Exit the corridor before re-entering ground-level play.
Do not sacrifice safety to reach an early loose ball.
Maintain midfield spacing outside the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether midfielders enter the corridor early.
The rucks’ approach and landing alignment.
Player awareness around the landing zone.
Timing of midfield entry after the tap.
Whether rucks exit safely before following the play.

commonErrors.error: Midfielder runs underneath the ruck.
commonErrors.correction: Begin wider and enter only after the rucks have landed.

commonErrors.error: Ruck jumps across the opponent’s corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a more vertical take-off and controlled forward line.

commonErrors.error: Players attack the loose ball before checking the landing.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise player safety and wait until the landing space clears.

commonErrors.error: Ruck remains inside the corridor after landing.
commonErrors.correction: Exit immediately before re-entering the contest.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders stand so wide they cannot reach the tap.
commonErrors.correction: Use angled starting positions that preserve access without entering the corridor.

progressions: Increase the opposing ruck to full controlled competition.
Remove the visible corridor markers.
Add controlled midfield defenders.
Vary the bounce or toss direction.
Add a time limit for the clearance.
regressions: Use one active ruck and one stationary marker.
successIndicators: Preserve clear approach and landing corridors.
matchApplication: Centre-bounce congestion can create dangerous landing situations when midfielders move underneath the rucks. Clear movement corridors protect players while still allowing the midfield group to attack the intended hit zone.
relatedDrills: RK-031 – Curved Approach Against Moving Opposition
RK-035 – Midfield Rotation Around the Ruck

title: Ruck Release Handball Under Pressure
primarySkill: Receiving and releasing under stoppage pressure
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to receive a follow-up handball in congestion, protect the football and release quickly to an available outside option.
groundSize: A 16 × 14-metre area with three release gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck contest.
Position one ruck, one inside midfielder and two outside receivers.
Add one controlled defender assigned to the ruck.
One feeder controls the toss.
Place three release gates around the area.
The defender may apply controlled body pressure but may not tackle until the ruck possesses the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder tosses the football.
The ruck taps towards the inside midfielder.
The ruck lands and moves into a support position.
The inside midfielder collects and handballs to the ruck.
The defender applies controlled pressure as the ruck receives.
The ruck protects the ball, scans and handballs to the available outside receiver.
The outside receiver exits through the nearest gate.
If the ruck is fully covered, the player may return the handball to the original midfielder.
If the defender wins possession, the defender exits through the opposite gate.
Rotate roles after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Move into support immediately after landing.
Present the hands early.
Scan outside options before receiving.
Receive with a stable base and body between the defender and football.
Keep the ball away from the defender’s reach.
Release quickly rather than absorbing unnecessary contact.
Use the safest available teammate.
Avoid turning blindly into pressure.
Transition immediately if the defender wins possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Timing of the ruck’s support movement.
Speed and accuracy of the release.
Selection of the correct outside option.
Whether the ruck holds the ball too long.

commonErrors.error: Ruck receives while stationary and upright.
commonErrors.correction: Move into the support lane and lower into a balanced receiving stance.

commonErrors.error: Player turns into the defender.
commonErrors.correction: Scan early and receive side-on to the pressure.

commonErrors.error: Football is exposed away from the body.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the ball protected on the far side from the defender.

commonErrors.error: Ruck holds possession too long.
commonErrors.correction: Release to the first safe option.

commonErrors.error: Player forces the preferred outside receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Use the free teammate or return option.

progressions: Allow full controlled tackling.
Add a second defender.
Remove the marked support lanes.
Vary the original tap direction.
Require the outside player to finish with a kick.
regressions: Begin with the ruck already positioned as the support player.
successIndicators: Follow into a useful support position.
matchApplication: Rucks often receive a return handball while surrounded by opponents. Strong body position and quick decision making allow the ruck to act as a link without becoming trapped in congestion.
relatedDrills: RK-035 – Midfield Rotation Around the Ruck

title: Continuous Stoppage Role-Switch Game
primarySkill: Adapting roles across continuous stoppages
objective: Develop the group’s ability to switch ruck, rover, support and defensive roles during a continuous sequence of changing stoppages.
groundSize: A 35 × 30-metre area containing five stoppage points.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark five stoppage points across the area.
Divide players into two evenly matched teams.
Each team nominates an initial ruck, inside midfielder, outside midfielder and defensive midfielder.
The coach holds several footballs.
Four scoring gates are positioned around the area.
Contact remains controlled and appropriate to the group.
The coach may nominate a new ruck before any stoppage.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach calls the first stoppage number and places or tosses a football there.
Teams organise immediately and contest the stoppage.
The team winning possession attempts to complete two disposals and exit through any scoring gate.
When the ball exits, is turned over or becomes locked in, the coach calls a new stoppage number.
Players relocate immediately.
Before selected stoppages, the coach calls a player’s name to become the new ruck.
The previous ruck must assume a midfield or support role.
Teams score one point for a clean clearance and one bonus point if the ruck contributes after the tap.
Play continues for three-minute rounds.
Allow ninety seconds of recovery and role discussion between rounds.
Complete three to four rounds.
coachingPoints: Communicate roles while travelling to the next contest.
Nominate the ruck clearly.
Preserve balanced midfield structure despite role changes.
Non-specialist rucks should use safe, controlled technique.
Follow the football after every tap.
React immediately when possession changes.
Spread towards available scoring gates.
Maintain decision quality as fatigue increases.
Avoid reckless jumping or contact late in rounds.
Use short recovery discussions to correct structure.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Speed and clarity of role nomination.
Whether players repeatedly assume familiar roles instead of adapting.
Contact intensity late in each round.

commonErrors.error: Players arrive without a nominated ruck.
commonErrors.correction: Name the role immediately while relocating.

commonErrors.error: Previous ruck remains outside the midfield structure.
commonErrors.correction: Assume a clear support or defensive responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Non-specialist ruck jumps unsafely.
commonErrors.correction: Use a controlled standing or low-jump technique.

commonErrors.error: All players chase the next stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish inside, outside and defensive spacing.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes reckless contact.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce intensity, increase recovery and reinforce controlled contest rules.

commonErrors.error: Team stops after a turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Transition immediately towards the nearest defensive gate.

progressions: Increase to match-like contact where appropriate.
Shorten recovery between rounds.
Remove visible stoppage numbers.
Add scoreboard scenarios.
Require different players to ruck at consecutive contests.
Expand to half-ground play.
regressions: Keep the same ruck for each round.
successIndicators: Nominate and accept new roles quickly.
Preserve communication and decision quality under fatigue.
matchApplication: In matches, injuries, rotations, mismatches and transition can leave different players contesting consecutive stoppages. Teams that reorganise quickly are less vulnerable when the designated ruck is unavailable or caught away from the contest.
relatedDrills: RK-030 – Ruck Movement and Connection Assessment
RK-035 – Midfield Rotation Around the Ruck

title: Movement and Re-Engagement Assessment
primarySkill: Assessment of ruck movement and re-engagement
objective: Assess whether players can move into, through and away from ruck contests safely while maintaining tactical connection, follow-up effort and role clarity.
groundSize: Approximately one-third of the ground containing four assessment stations.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create four assessment stations.
Station 1: curved approach, changing opposition position and aborted leap decisions.
Station 2: long tap, chase, ground-ball recovery and follow-up pressure.
Station 3: midfield rotation, boundary front-or-back read and clearance connection.
Station 4: centre-bounce landing corridors and continuous role switching.
Divide players evenly between stations.
Assign an observer to each station where possible.
Use the ratings developing, competent and advanced.
Modify jump, contact and running loads for age, injury status and masters players.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete six to eight minutes at each station.
At Station 1, each ruck performs six changing approach contests and must demonstrate at least one safe abandoned leap.
At Station 2, players complete four long-tap chases and four defensive follow-up efforts.
At Station 3, groups complete front and rear boundary connections following a midfield rotation.
At Station 4, players demonstrate safe centre-bounce movement before completing a continuous role-switch sequence.
Coaches assess technique, safety, decision making, communication and follow-up involvement.
Players rotate after the coach’s signal.
Each player receives one movement priority and one tactical re-engagement priority.
Finish with a four-minute continuous stoppage game using the station themes.
Retain assessment results for later comparison.
coachingPoints: Assess movement before, during and after the aerial contest.
Reward safe decisions when the planned jump or approach becomes unsuitable.
Evaluate whether players remain involved after an unsuccessful tap.
Observe legal pressure and body positioning.
Assess midfield movement around the ruck’s approach and landing space.
Include boundary and centre-bounce awareness.
Evaluate communication during role changes.
Reward adaptable decisions rather than rigid execution.
Monitor technique as fatigue increases.
Apply the same standards across all stations.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Balance when an opponent changes position.
Defensive pressure after a lost tap.

commonErrors.error: Assessment rewards only tap wins.
commonErrors.correction: Score movement, safety, direction, follow-up and team connection.

commonErrors.error: Player completes unsafe jumps to appear competitive.
commonErrors.correction: Reward correct grounded decisions and remove points for poor balance.

commonErrors.error: Ruck becomes inactive after the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Include second-effort involvement in every station score.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders interfere with approach or landing space.
commonErrors.correction: Reset starting positions and preserve clear movement corridors.

commonErrors.error: Players lose role clarity during the final game.
commonErrors.correction: Require immediate verbal role nomination.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes uncontrolled contact.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce repetition volume or increase recovery before continuing.

progressions: Repeat the assessment with live controlled opposition.
Remove visible movement corridors and hit zones.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Compare results with RK-020 and RK-030.
Use video review for individual feedback.
Expand the final activity to half-ground match simulation.
regressions: Keep visible approach, hit-zone and landing markers.
successIndicators: Recognise when to jump or remain grounded.
Follow long taps and loose footballs.
Apply effective pressure after losing possession.
Connect boundary taps with available receivers.
Maintain technique and decision quality under movement and fatigue.
matchApplication: The assessment determines whether players can transfer technical ruck skills into dynamic match movement. It identifies who can enter contests safely, adapt when conditions change and remain tactically useful after the initial tap.
relatedDrills: RK-031 – Curved Approach Against Moving Opposition
RK-032 – Aborted Leap and Grounded Re-Contest
RK-035 – Midfield Rotation Around the Ruck
RK-038 – Ruck Release Handball Under Pressure

title: Opposed Tap to the Protected Side
primarySkill: Directing a tap away from opposition pressure
objective: Develop the ruck’s ability to identify the protected side of an opposed contest and direct the football away from the opponent’s strongest influence.
groundSize: A 12 × 12-metre contest area with two opposing hit zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck contest.
Place one hit-zone gate on each side of the contest.
Position one ruck and one opposing ruck at the central point.
Place one midfielder behind each hit zone.
One feeder stands four metres away.
The defender begins with a slight positional advantage towards one side.
Contact is limited to legal body positioning and controlled shoulder or side pressure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder identifies which ruck is attacking.
Before the toss, the attacking ruck scans the opponent’s position.
The feeder tosses the football vertically.
The attacking ruck competes for first contact and attempts to direct the football towards the side least influenced by the opponent.
The opposing ruck attempts to deny that space or neutralise the tap.
The corresponding midfielder moves late to collect.
Both rucks land and follow the football.
The midfielder exits through the hit-zone gate.
Players swap attacking and defensive roles after four contests.
Award one point for selecting the correct protected side and one point for a controlled connection.
coachingPoints: Scan the opponent’s stance, hips and tapping hand before the toss.
Avoid committing to a target before identifying the pressure side.
Use body position to preserve access to the protected space.
Keep the tapping hand open and finish towards the selected zone.
Do not force a long tap when a short protected drop is available.
Maintain balance through controlled contact.
The midfielder should hold space until the tap direction becomes clear.
Follow the tap immediately after landing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the attacking ruck scans before the contest.
The relationship between opponent position and target selection.
Whether the player forces the preferred hand or side.

commonErrors.error: Ruck taps towards the opponent’s strongest position.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the opponent’s alignment and use the opposite protected side.

commonErrors.error: Player commits to the target before the toss.
commonErrors.correction: Hold a neutral position until the football and opponent are read.

commonErrors.error: Ruck uses excessive force to escape pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use controlled touch into the available space.

commonErrors.error: Midfielder enters the zone too early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the starting position and move after the tap becomes identifiable.

commonErrors.error: Ruck stops after contact.
commonErrors.correction: Land and follow towards the receiving midfielder.

progressions: Allow the defender to change position immediately before the toss.
Remove the visible target gates.
Add a second midfielder and defender.
Allow the attacking ruck to use either a short or long protected tap.
Begin from a boundary throw-in position.
successIndicators: Deliver a controllable tap under pressure.
matchApplication: Opposing rucks frequently protect a preferred hand or hit zone. Reading that position and tapping to the protected side reduces interception risk and gives midfielders a clearer path to first possession.
relatedDrills: RK-031 – Curved Approach Against Moving Opposition

title: Contact Entry and Balance Recovery
primarySkill: Maintaining balance through initial ruck contact
objective: Teach rucks to absorb controlled contact during the approach, recover their base and remain capable of making a safe and effective contest.
groundSize: A 12 × 8-metre approach and contest lane.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a five-metre ruck approach lane.
Place a central take-off area at the end of the lane.
One ruck begins at the approach marker.
One pressure player begins beside the final two metres of the lane.
One feeder stands beside the take-off area.
The pressure player may apply one controlled shoulder or side contact.
Holding, extended-arm pushing, high contact and contact from behind are prohibited.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ruck begins a controlled approach.
The pressure player moves alongside and applies one legal body contact.
The ruck absorbs the pressure using a stable base and short recovery steps.
The feeder tosses the football immediately after contact.
The ruck decides whether to jump or remain grounded.
The player palms the football towards a target gate.
The ruck lands and holds balance for one second before following the ball.
Complete four repetitions from each side.
Rotate all roles.
Award one point for balance recovery and one point for a clean contest.
coachingPoints: Expect contact without bracing rigidly.
Keep the knees and hips flexed.
Absorb pressure through the feet and torso.
Use short recovery steps rather than crossing the feet.
Maintain visual contact with the football.
Do not retaliate with extended arms.
Reassess whether jumping remains safe after contact.
Prioritise balance before attempting direction.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ruck remains relaxed before contact.
The width of the player’s base.
Whether the player loses sight of the ball.
The decision to jump or stay grounded.

commonErrors.error: Ruck stiffens and is displaced easily.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain flexion through the ankles, knees and hips.

commonErrors.error: Player crosses the feet after contact.
commonErrors.correction: Use short recovery steps and rebuild the base.

commonErrors.error: Ruck pushes back with an extended arm.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the arms inside the body line and recover through footwork.

commonErrors.error: Player jumps while off balance.
commonErrors.correction: Remain grounded until a stable contest position is restored.

commonErrors.error: Pressure player makes forceful or late contact.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce intensity and restrict contact to one legal side engagement.

progressions: Vary the timing of the contact.
Allow the pressure player to approach from either legal side.
Add a passive opposing ruck at the ball.
Add a moving hit-zone target.
Progress to a fully opposed contest.
regressions: Apply contact from a stationary position.
Announce the contact side before the approach.
successIndicators: Absorb controlled contact without falling or crossing the feet.
Complete the tap and landing under control.
matchApplication: Rucks regularly experience legal body pressure before reaching the ball. Recovering balance without retaliating or forcing an unsafe jump allows the player to remain competitive and reduces the risk of late collision or poor landing.
relatedDrills: RK-031 – Curved Approach Against Moving Opposition
RK-032 – Aborted Leap and Grounded Re-Contest
RK-041 – Opposed Tap to the Protected Side

title: Late Contact Tap Control
primarySkill: Maintaining tap control under late legal pressure
objective: Develop the ability to preserve safe hand shape and tap direction when controlled legal pressure is applied immediately before or during the aerial contest.
groundSize: An 8 × 8-metre contest area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark one central take-off area.
Place two target hoops three metres away.
One ruck stands or begins with a one-step approach.
One pressure player starts beside the ruck.
One feeder delivers a consistent vertical toss.
The pressure player may apply controlled side or shoulder pressure after the ruck begins the jump.
No pushing in the back, high contact or undercutting is permitted.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder calls one target and tosses the football.
The ruck approaches or prepares to jump.
The pressure player applies controlled legal contact as the ruck rises.
The ruck maintains visual contact and an open palm.
The player directs the football towards the called target.
Both players land in their own space.
The ruck follows the football for three metres.
Complete four contests from each side before rotating.
Award one point for safe control and one point for an accurate tap.
coachingPoints: Keep the tapping shoulder and hand relaxed before contact.
Stabilise through the trunk rather than swinging the free arm.
Maintain an open hand throughout the contest.
Accept a shorter tap when pressure limits full extension.
Avoid twisting across the opponent.
Keep the eyes on the football through contact.
Land with feet apart and knees flexed.
Stop the activity immediately if pressure becomes unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether contact changes the ruck’s hand shape.
Whether the player overreaches after being displaced.
Contact intensity from the pressure player.

commonErrors.error: Ruck closes the hand and punches the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain an open palm and accept a shorter controlled contact.

commonErrors.error: Free arm swings into the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the elbow bent and the arm near the body.

commonErrors.error: Player twists dangerously in the air.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the target angle and stabilise the torso.

commonErrors.error: Ruck overreaches after losing position.
commonErrors.correction: Use the best safe contact available rather than forcing full extension.

commonErrors.error: Pressure player contacts from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Restrict pressure to legal shoulder or side contact.

progressions: Vary the target after take-off begins.
Add a moving midfielder.
Allow the pressure player to contest the football.
Increase approach distance.
Use a boundary throw-in delivery.
regressions: Apply contact with a soft pad.
Use standing reaches rather than jumps.
successIndicators: Keep body control under legal pressure.
Avoid unsafe arm or torso movement.
Land safely and follow the play.
matchApplication: Even when a ruck reaches the football first, late legal pressure can reduce extension and accuracy. Maintaining hand shape and body control allows the player to create a useful result rather than an uncontrolled knock.
relatedDrills: RK-015 – Tap Weight and Distance Control
RK-042 – Contact Entry and Balance Recovery

title: Ruck Re-Contest Ground-Ball Battle
primarySkill: Re-contesting the football after a neutral tap
objective: Develop the ability of both rucks to transition immediately from an aerial neutralisation into a balanced ground-level contest.
groundSize: A 10 × 10-metre contest square with two exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central ruck point.
Place two exit gates five metres away.
Position two rucks at the contest.
One feeder delivers the football.
One support player waits beyond each gate.
The feeder or coach instructs both rucks to deaden the initial tap into a nearby ground-ball zone.
Controlled body contact is permitted after both players land.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder tosses the football.
Both rucks compete but aim to keep the football within two metres of the contest.
As soon as the ball reaches ground level, both players recover their landing.
The rucks compete to collect, knock or protect the loose football.
The player gaining possession handballs to the support player at either gate.
The losing ruck applies controlled pressure.
If neither player gains possession within five seconds, the feeder resets the contest.
Complete six repetitions before rotating support and feeder roles.
Award one point for first clean ground possession and one point for a successful release.
coachingPoints: Land before lowering into the ground-ball contest.
Locate the football immediately.
Approach the ground ball with the body behind its path.
Keep the feet active under body pressure.
Protect the football without holding the opponent.
Use a quick handball once possession is secured.
Continue applying legal pressure after losing the ball.
Avoid diving underneath an airborne or landing player.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Speed of transition to ground level.
Whether players dive dangerously into the landing space.
Repeat pressure from the losing player.

commonErrors.error: Player bends at the waist and reaches.
commonErrors.correction: Lower through the hips and knees with the body behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Ruck attacks the ball before the opponent has landed.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the landing space and enter once both players are grounded.
